Minisforum’s UM750 Neo is an unusual mini PC not because it uses an AMD chip, but because it uses the standard Ryzen Z1: a processor AMD designed for handheld gaming systems. That decision makes the UM750 Neo harder to judge by a simple specification checklist. Its compact-PC fundamentals look practical—fixed 16GB memory, two SSD slots, USB4, 2.5GbE, Wi-Fi 6E and support for three displays—but the Z1 is also a notably cut-down graphics configuration beside the better-known Z1 Extreme. The result could be a capable small Windows machine for general work and lighter gaming, yet the published price makes it essential to avoid assuming it is a bargain gaming box before independent testing arrives.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Futuristic mini PC showcased with processor, memory, connectivity, gaming displays, cooling, and performance graphics."]178313[/ATTACH]
[HEADING=1]It is a product listing, not just an IFA preview[/HEADING]
The UM750 Neo appeared on Minisforum’s IFA 2026 material with a concise specification: AMD Z1, 16GB of LPDDR5 memory and two PCIe 4.0 M.2 slots, labeled “Coming Soon.” That label remains relevant for the event page, but it does not describe availability everywhere.
Official regional listings have already supplied considerably more detail. In the United States, Minisforum lists two systems: a 16GB/500GB model at $463 and a 16GB/1TB model at $535. Both had an estimated shipping window of late September as of September 7. In Japan, Minisforum lists a 16GB/500GB configuration at ¥79,999 and says it is scheduled to ship on September 15.
China appears to be further along, at least according to a September 3 report that described sales through JD. The reported configurations were barebones at 2,399 yuan, 16GB/500GB at 2,999 yuan, and 16GB/1TB at 3,599 yuan.
That patchwork matters for prospective buyers. “Coming Soon” on a global promotional page should not be read as a universal launch date, and a price in one region should not be treated as a direct price promise in another. The published U.S. and Japanese figures also represent observed storefront pricing, not proof of a permanent MSRP or of identical availability through third-party sellers. Shipping estimates are estimates, not confirmation that units have reached customers.
[HEADING=1]The platform: strong connectivity, fixed memory, uneven SSD bandwidth[/HEADING]
The basics are better specified than the early announcement suggested. The UM750 Neo carries 16GB of LPDDR5-6400 memory integrated onto the motherboard. For Windows users, “onboard” is the important word: the stated memory configuration should be approached as fixed rather than as an upgradeable SO-DIMM setup. Buyers who know they need more than 16GB for local virtual machines, large creative projects, heavier development environments, or aggressive multitasking should not assume they can solve that limitation later.
For everyday Windows use, 16GB is a credible baseline. It leaves room for a browser, Office-style applications, video calls, background sync utilities and modest creative work. The constraint becomes more meaningful when memory is shared with integrated graphics. A game or GPU-accelerated workload has to coexist with Windows and applications within that same pool, so usable headroom can tighten sooner than it would on a desktop with separate graphics memory.
Storage is one of the more appealing aspects, but it has a qualification that deserves more attention than the phrase “dual PCIe 4.0 M.2” normally receives. Minisforum specifies two M.2 2280 SSD slots, with stated total support up to 8TB—up to 4TB per drive. One slot uses PCIe 4.0 x4, while the other is PCIe 4.0 x2.
That does not make the second slot unhelpful. It remains valuable for separating a Windows installation from a game library, media collection, project files or backup-oriented storage without needing an external drive. But the two slots are not equal. The x2 slot has fewer PCIe lanes, which can constrain peak transfer performance relative to the x4 slot when the SSD and workload can use the additional bandwidth. The sensible build order is therefore straightforward: put the operating system and the most demanding storage workload on the x4 slot, and use the x2 slot for capacity or less performance-sensitive data.
The system’s published connectivity also includes USB4, 2.5GbE networking, Wi-Fi 6E and three display outputs. For a desk-bound Windows setup, these features may matter more than the processor’s handheld origin. USB4 broadens the range of high-speed dock and storage possibilities, 2.5GbE can be useful on a fast local network or NAS, and three display outputs make a compact multi-monitor workstation plausible. Exact experience will still depend on display resolutions, refresh rates, docks, cables, drivers and the workloads being run; the headline count alone does not establish every multi-display combination.
[HEADING=1]What the regular Ryzen Z1 changes[/HEADING]
AMD introduced the Ryzen Z1 family for handheld PC gaming, and AMD classifies the standard Z1’s form factor as handheld. The regular Z1 has six CPU cores and 12 threads, boosts up to 4.9GHz, and contains four RDNA 3 graphics cores.
Those CPU specifications mean it should not automatically be dismissed as a low-end Windows processor. Six modern CPU cores and 12 threads can suit routine desktop computing, web-heavy workloads and many productivity tasks. A mini PC also operates in a fundamentally different physical setting than a battery-powered handheld: it is normally connected to wall power and may have more room for cooling. But neither point tells us how Minisforum configured the UM750 Neo’s power limits, fan profile or sustained clocks.
The graphics side is where comparisons require the greatest care. AMD’s Z1 Extreme carries 12 RDNA 3 graphics cores, triple the four listed for the standard Z1. That is not a minor branding distinction. It is a major reduction in graphics resources, and it creates a clear reason to moderate gaming expectations.
Controlled testing in otherwise comparable ROG Ally handhelds illustrates the scale of the gap. In the tested settings, the Z1 Extreme led the standard Z1 by 42% on battery and 52% on wall power in [I]Dying Light 2[/I]. In [I]Resident Evil 4[/I], the reported advantages were 36% on battery and 48% on wall power.
Those results are useful context, not UM750 Neo benchmark results. A mini PC can differ from a handheld in cooling, power delivery, firmware, memory behavior, storage configuration and driver state. The figures cannot responsibly be converted into a promised frame rate for any game on Minisforum’s machine. What they do establish is the direction and potential importance of the product split: graphics-limited games can run materially better on Z1 Extreme hardware than on regular-Z1 hardware under comparable conditions.
[HEADING=1]A realistic Windows and gaming role[/HEADING]
The most defensible early positioning for the UM750 Neo is as a compact general-purpose Windows PC with room for lighter gaming, older titles, esports-oriented games, indie releases and settings compromises where needed. Its dual-drive capacity, wired networking and display support could also make it appealing as a small living-room machine, a compact office desktop or a home lab-adjacent system where 16GB of non-upgradeable memory is enough.
It is less safe to position it as a substitute for a higher-end gaming mini PC solely because it contains a chip from AMD’s handheld line. The regular Z1’s four RDNA 3 graphics cores set a much different expectation from Z1 Extreme systems. Demanding modern games, high resolutions, high settings and ambitious multi-tasking alongside gaming are precisely the areas where prospective buyers should wait for actual UM750 Neo measurements.
There are other unanswered practical questions. No independent hands-on review or benchmark of this specific mini PC was available in the supplied information. That means there is no verified evidence yet on sustained CPU or GPU performance, power limits, operating temperatures, fan noise, SSD compatibility, sleep behavior, Wi-Fi performance or real-world display and USB4 behavior. The compact enclosure could be well tuned, but it could also expose limits that a processor specification cannot reveal.
For buyers who need a quiet PC or who plan to put two high-capacity SSDs inside, those omissions are especially important. A full review should test performance after extended load rather than just short benchmark bursts, compare fan behavior at idle and under gaming load, and verify whether both NVMe slots remain practical under thermal pressure.
[HEADING=1]The price asks for comparison, not assumptions[/HEADING]
At $463 for the 16GB/500GB U.S. configuration and $535 for the 16GB/1TB version, the UM750 Neo is not established as an ultra-cheap mini PC. It may be competitively priced in particular markets or sales periods, but there is no market-wide comparison in the available evidence that supports calling it one of the least expensive mini PCs.
That distinction is important because the processor choice has invited speculation that AMD may be moving leftover Z1 inventory into mini PCs. There is no evidence provided for that claim: no AMD statement, inventory data, shipment data or independent reporting establishes such a motive. It should be treated as conjecture, not an explanation for the product.
Instead, buyers should make a direct comparison against alternatives available in their region at the time of purchase. Prioritize the complete system, not only the processor name: fixed versus upgradeable memory, storage capacity, warranty terms, port selection, networking, noise expectations and independently measured performance all affect value. A lower upfront price can be less attractive if 16GB becomes restrictive and cannot be expanded; conversely, the integrated 16GB may be entirely adequate for a small desktop intended for mainstream Windows work.
[HEADING=1]Z1 arrives in a newer Z-series landscape[/HEADING]
Timing also complicates the appeal. AMD’s current handheld lineup includes newer Z2-family products, including Ryzen Z2 Extreme and Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme, alongside Z1 and Z1 Extreme. AMD announced the Z2 series in January 2025, and the announced Z2 Extreme specification included eight CPU cores, 16 threads and 16 RDNA 3.5 graphics cores.
That makes the UM750 Neo’s Z1 a previous-generation choice within AMD’s handheld-focused stack. It does not make the mini PC obsolete by definition. Product usefulness depends on price, actual implementation and the user’s needs. A compact, connected Windows system does not need to lead a gaming benchmark chart to be worthwhile.
Still, its place in the range is clear: buyers should expect the UM750 Neo to compete on compact design and system features rather than assume that the Z1 label grants it the graphics credentials of newer or Extreme-tier AMD designs. There is also insufficient evidence to make sweeping claims about how widely each Z-series chip has been adopted across the handheld market.
[HEADING=1]Who should wait and who can consider it[/HEADING]
The UM750 Neo is already sufficiently specified for a narrow kind of buyer to take it seriously: someone who wants a very small Windows desktop, accepts 16GB as a permanent memory ceiling, values two internal M.2 slots and fast connectivity, and views gaming as secondary or adjustable rather than as the central requirement.
Buyers seeking the best integrated-graphics performance, a quiet under-load system, flexible memory upgrades, or confidence in demanding game performance should wait for independent UM750 Neo testing. The available handheld comparisons make one point clear without overreaching: the standard Ryzen Z1 is not interchangeable with the Z1 Extreme where graphics performance is the limiting factor.
Minisforum has turned a handheld-class processor into a more expandable desktop-style system. Whether that combination is compelling will depend less on the novelty of the chip and more on the unanswered details: sustained performance, acoustics, thermals, firmware quality and whether regional street pricing brings the machine into line with the modest graphics hardware it contains.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
A striking homelab project has given an HP ProLiant MicroServer N40L a second life—but not in the usual sense of upgrading an old server. EastMakes has replaced the original computing platform with a purpose-built carrier board for Raspberry Pi’s Compute Module 5 (CM5), shaped and connected for the N40L chassis. It is an inventive example of hardware reuse, yet its practical limits matter as much as its clean fit: the old chassis is demonstrably being reused, while the old AMD motherboard, processor, and DDR3 memory are not.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Open computer case reveals internal circuit boards, wiring, cooling fan, and drive bays beside a motherboard."]178312[/ATTACH]
That distinction is important for anyone evaluating the project as a template for a home NAS, small server, or Windows-adjacent lab machine. This is not an ordinary drop-in CPU upgrade, nor is the CM5 itself a standalone motherboard. It is a bespoke ARM-based platform that happens to make unusually good use of a compact, purpose-built server enclosure.
[HEADING=1]What has changed inside the MicroServer[/HEADING]
The original HP ProLiant MicroServer N40L was built around AMD’s Turion II Neo N40L processor running at 1.5 GHz. HPE specified two slots for PC3-10600E unbuffered DDR3 ECC memory, with 8 GB as the maximum supported configuration. Its platform also included embedded SATA RAID 0/1 and a 150 W non-redundant power supply.
EastMakes’ project removes that original motherboard-level platform. The builder described taking the Compute Module 5 IO Board reference design and turning it into a custom motherboard specifically for the N40L chassis. In other words, the project keeps the enclosure and adapts a modern embedded computer platform to it; it does not preserve the N40L’s AMD processor, memory, onboard SATA controller, or original motherboard.
The finished board reportedly includes an M.2 NVMe SSD, Ethernet and USB ports arranged to meet the case’s existing rear I/O openings, and a white 24-pin power connector intended to connect to the old power supply. The board also has front-edge switches labelled “Boop” and “Re-Boop,” an appropriately playful reminder that this is a custom-maker project rather than an official HPE replacement assembly.
This is a better description of a chassis conversion than a revival of the original server hardware. That is not a criticism. Retaining a well-designed enclosure, its physical layout, and potentially its power and cooling infrastructure can be more useful than discarding the entire system. But it does alter what users should expect from it.
[HEADING=1]Why CM5 needs a custom carrier board[/HEADING]
The Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 is not a connector-equipped Raspberry Pi motherboard. Raspberry Pi describes it as similar to a Raspberry Pi without the physical connectors, with the companion CM5IO carrier supplying those connections. That makes it suitable for custom embedded designs, but it also means the carrier board determines much of the completed system’s I/O, power design, mechanical arrangement, and expansion path.
At its core, CM5 includes a quad-core 2.4 GHz Cortex-A76 processor, integrated Gigabit Ethernet PHY, and one PCIe Gen 2 ×1 host interface. Those specifications make it a substantially different class of platform from the N40L’s older AMD system. However, they do not, by themselves, establish a measured performance lead in any particular workload.
No supplied CPU, memory, network, storage, thermal, power-use, or real-world application benchmarks compare the custom CM5 system with the stock N40L. A claim that it delivers a major performance upgrade would therefore be plausible in some tasks but unproven by the available evidence. Clock speeds alone cannot compare processors of different designs, architectures, and generations, and server usefulness depends heavily on the workload, storage topology, software stack, and sustained stability.
For Windows and PC enthusiasts, architecture is another major dividing line. The original system used an AMD x86 processor; the replacement is ARMv8-based. The available project information does not identify an operating system, boot arrangement, or application stack. It consequently provides no basis to promise a particular Windows installation experience, Windows application compatibility, driver availability, virtualization workflow, or migration route from software used on the original machine. Treat it as a custom ARM server build, not as an x86 MicroServer with newer internals.
[HEADING=1]NVMe is useful, but expansion is tightly bounded[/HEADING]
The M.2 NVMe SSD is among the most consequential parts of the build. Raspberry Pi’s CM5IO reference design provides an M.2 M-key PCIe socket for NVMe SSDs, and EastMakes’ design follows that general platform approach.
The ceiling is important: CM5 exposes one PCIe Gen 2 ×1 host link, documented at 5 Gb/s. The CM5IO design’s default M.2 connection is likewise PCIe Gen 2 ×1. That is a useful interface for solid-state storage in a compact server, but it is not comparable to the multi-lane PCIe connections common in recent desktop or server systems. The available PCIe link is shared at the platform-design level: a custom carrier based on CM5 has only that one host connection unless the designer adds switching or makes another design change.
That affects both expectations and future expansion. An NVMe drive can provide a responsive boot and application volume, but the project does not establish its actual throughput, latency, boot source, or sustained behavior. The exact SSD model is also undocumented. More importantly, using the lone PCIe lane for NVMe limits straightforward access to other PCIe-attached hardware.
The four front drive bays are the central reason many people still appreciate the N40L chassis, but their present role in this build should not be overstated. The builder indicated that the installed SSD could later be removed and replaced with an M.2-to-SAS adapter when hard-drive prices normalize. This suggests a possible path to reconnecting the enclosure’s drive bays, but it is not evidence that the current configuration operates a four-drive SATA or SAS backplane.
That distinction has real consequences for a NAS plan. A single NVMe-based setup can be useful for a lightweight server, but it is not the same as a documented multi-drive storage appliance with established drive-bay connectivity. An M.2-to-SAS option could be compelling, but it would also place storage expansion behind the same single PCIe Gen 2 ×1 host interface and requires an implementation not yet documented here.
[HEADING=1]The power integration is clever, not yet verified[/HEADING]
The white 24-pin connector is one of the most visually persuasive aspects of the conversion. It is reportedly intended to connect the custom board to the N40L’s existing power supply, potentially avoiding a loose external power brick and helping the converted machine retain the tidy, appliance-like quality of the original chassis.
Yet electrical integration is the area where visual success should not be mistaken for validation. Raspberry Pi’s reference CM5IO design is designed around external 5 V input. The available material does not include the custom board’s full schematic, its voltage-rail design, component list, conversion details, or sustained-load electrical measurements. There is also no independent rail analysis confirming that the connector safely and correctly supplies the carrier’s requirements through the original server PSU.
That does not mean the implementation is faulty. It means outside observers do not currently have enough evidence to declare it trouble-free. Builders considering a similar modification should treat PSU compatibility as a design and test problem, not as an assumption derived from connector shape or successful initial operation. Power stability, thermal behavior, protection circuitry, and behavior under storage and USB load all remain material unknowns.
[HEADING=1]Signal integrity remains an open engineering question[/HEADING]
The builder has also offered an unusually useful caveat: PCIe may be experiencing errors “under the hood,” but the necessary equipment to test it was unavailable. This is not a trivial footnote. PCIe routing and signal integrity are central to dependable NVMe storage and any later PCIe-to-SAS design.
Raspberry Pi documents PCIe Gen 2 operation for CM5 and cautions that Gen 3 operation is unsupported and might not work reliably. The carrier’s intended Gen 2 ×1 link is therefore the relevant target. Even at that supported mode, however, a custom board needs validation if it is to graduate from a promising prototype to a server trusted with important data.
A machine can appear normal in light testing while exhibiting intermittent storage faults, resets, or corruption risks during heavier and longer-running workloads. The available evidence does not show that those problems exist; equally, it does not rule them out. The sensible conclusion is that extended testing is still needed before treating the conversion as a proven always-on storage platform.
[HEADING=1]What the project demonstrates—and what it does not[/HEADING]
EastMakes has demonstrated something genuinely interesting: an off-the-shelf Compute Module reference design can be transformed into a chassis-specific motherboard that uses the physical design of an old MicroServer far more elegantly than a generic single-board-computer installation. Rear I/O alignment, internal NVMe storage, and a direct-looking power connection show the value of designing around a particular enclosure rather than merely fitting parts wherever space permits.
The conversion also illustrates a more sustainable route for obsolete hardware. The N40L’s original computational limits need not condemn its chassis to recycling when a new low-power computing platform can be designed around it. For homelab users, that can be an appealing alternative to buying a wholly new compact server.
But several claims remain premature. There is no comparative benchmark record showing how much faster the finished system is than the original N40L. There is no published proof of continuous PCIe reliability, no confirmed power-rail validation, and no documented current connection between the custom board and all four front drive bays. Nor is there evidence in the available project material of a release plan, cost, production-ready files, or a supported product for other N40L owners to buy.
The best way to view the build, then, is as a promising custom carrier-board prototype and a thoughtful chassis-reuse exercise. It is not yet a verified recipe for a high-performance four-bay NAS, a drop-in replacement motherboard, or a universal modernisation path for old x86 home servers. Those interested in copying the idea should prioritize electrical and long-duration storage testing, understand the one-lane PCIe constraint, and avoid making operating-system assumptions that the project has not documented.
That measured view does not diminish the accomplishment. It clarifies why the project is interesting: it turns a familiar retired server case into a platform for new engineering, while exposing exactly how much engineering is required to make old hardware reuse dependable rather than merely clever.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
Windows 10 and Windows 11 can use a local security group to turn a recurring permissions chore into one change: add a user to the group once, then grant the group access to the folders, printers, or SMB shares it needs. Microsoft’s Local Accounts documentation confirms that Computer Management, [ICODE]NET.EXE LOCALGROUP[/ICODE], and the [ICODE]Microsoft.PowerShell.LocalAccounts[/ICODE] cmdlets all manage the same class of local group membership. The important limitation is scope: a local group exists on [B]one Windows PC[/B], not across every PC in an organization.
That makes local groups ideal for a shared workstation, a small office file server, a lab machine, or a standalone PC hosting an SMB share. It is less appropriate for a domain-joined fleet already managed through Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID and Intune, where centrally managed groups avoid duplicating membership on each endpoint.
The useful pattern is simple. Create a group such as [ICODE]ProjectEditors[/ICODE], put the appropriate accounts in it, and grant [ICODE]ProjectEditors[/ICODE] Modify permission to a working folder. When someone joins or leaves the project, change group membership rather than editing the folder’s access control list for every individual account.
[HEADING=1][ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Windows shows ProjectEditors group setup with NTFS and SMB permissions for shared project files."]178310[/ATTACH]Check the Windows edition before opening Computer Management[/HEADING]
On supported Windows 10 and Windows 11 editions, right-click Start and choose [B]Computer Management[/B], then expand [B]System Tools[/B]. The graphical [I]Local Users and Groups[/I] node can also be opened directly with [ICODE]lusrmgr.msc[/ICODE].
Microsoft documents Computer Management as the MMC console for managing local accounts. In practice, the Local Users and Groups snap-in is normally present on Windows Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions. It is deliberately absent from Windows Home. If [ICODE]lusrmgr.msc[/ICODE] reports that the snap-in cannot be used, or the node is missing from Computer Management, that is usually an edition limitation rather than a damaged Windows installation.
Before proceeding, confirm the edition in [B]Settings > System > About[/B]. Administrators must also use an account with local administrative rights to create groups, change membership, or alter permissions on protected folders.
There is another boundary worth keeping clear: do not use Local Users and Groups to administer accounts on a domain controller. Microsoft’s documentation explicitly excludes that scenario. On a member PC, a local group can contain local accounts and, depending on the environment, domain, Microsoft Entra, or Microsoft account identities—but the group itself remains local to that machine.
[HEADING=1]Create a group in Local Users and Groups[/HEADING]
In Computer Management, open [B]System Tools > Local Users and Groups > Groups[/B]. The pane already contains built-in groups such as Administrators, Users, Remote Desktop Users, and Backup Operators. Those groups can grant powerful operating-system rights, so a custom group is the safer choice when the only goal is access to a particular project folder or share.
Right-click an empty area in the Groups pane and select [B]New Group[/B]. Give it a descriptive, role-based name, such as [ICODE]ProjectEditors[/ICODE], [ICODE]AccountingReadOnly[/ICODE], or [ICODE]LabShareUsers[/ICODE]. Add a short description that says what access the group is meant to control and who approves membership. That small bit of documentation prevents a common administrative failure months later: nobody knows whether an old group is still needed, so it retains access indefinitely.
Select [B]Add[/B] to choose users or other principals. If the Select Users dialog is ambiguous, use [B]Locations[/B] to make sure the local computer is selected, then type the account name and choose [B]Check Names[/B]. A local identity can be written as [ICODE]COMPUTERNAME\username[/ICODE]; qualifying it this way is particularly useful on a domain-joined PC where a domain user has the same short name.
After saving the new group, open its Properties page and use the [B]Members[/B] tab to verify the result. Do not assume that adding a person to a group grants access immediately. The group still needs a permission entry on the resource, and a user already signed in may need to sign out and back in before a newly assigned token membership is reflected consistently.
Avoid treating custom groups as a shortcut into the built-in [B]Administrators[/B] group. Microsoft warns that Administrators members receive Full Control over the local computer. A folder-access group should be granted access to the folder, not elevated rights across Windows.
[HEADING=1]Grant the group folder access instead of individual access[/HEADING]
To apply the group to an NTFS folder, right-click the folder, select [B]Properties[/B], and open the [B]Security[/B] tab. Choose [B]Edit[/B], then [B]Add[/B], enter the local group name, and confirm it resolves to the local computer’s group. Assign the least privilege that meets the job:
[LIST]
[*][B]Read & execute[/B] works for users who only need to open files and run permitted content.
[*][B]Modify[/B] is usually the practical choice for a collaborative data folder because it allows users to create, change, and delete files.
[*][B]Full control[/B] should be reserved for administrators or owners who must change permissions and take ownership.
[/LIST]
For a normal shared working directory, grant [ICODE]ProjectEditors[/ICODE] [B]Modify[/B] and retain Full Control for local Administrators and SYSTEM. Then test with a standard account that belongs to the group. A permissions dialog that looks correct is not proof that the intended workflow works, especially when inheritance or older user-specific entries are involved.
The [B]Advanced[/B] button is where administrators should check whether the group’s access applies to “This folder, subfolders and files.” A permission assigned only to the top-level folder can allow users to browse it but fail when they attempt to create or edit files in child folders. Conversely, inherited permissions can expose more than intended if the group is added too high in the directory tree.
Use explicit [I]deny[/I] entries sparingly. Windows evaluates access control entries in a defined order, and an explicit denial can override a broad allow inherited through another group. In most small deployments, it is clearer and safer to remove an unnecessary allow permission than to build a tangle of denies.
Microsoft’s [ICODE]icacls[/ICODE] documentation identifies it as the supported command-line tool for viewing and modifying NTFS discretionary access control lists. This is a useful verification step after GUI changes:
[ICODE]icacls 'D:\TeamFiles'[/ICODE]
To grant a local group Modify rights recursively to the folder, files, and subfolders, run an elevated 64-bit Windows PowerShell session:
[CODE]$Group = "$env:COMPUTERNAME\ProjectEditors"
icacls 'D:\TeamFiles' /grant "${Group}:(OI)(CI)M"[/CODE]
[ICODE](OI)(CI)[/ICODE] makes the permission inherit to files and child folders; [ICODE]M[/ICODE] means Modify. Use this deliberately: inheritance is powerful, and applying it to an existing folder tree changes the security posture of everything beneath it.
[HEADING=1]An SMB share has two permission layers[/HEADING]
A group can also control a network share, but Windows has two separate checks: the SMB [B]share permission[/B] and the NTFS permission on the underlying folder. Network users must satisfy both. Granting Modify on the folder alone does not help if the share permission allows only Read; granting Change on the share alone does not bypass a restrictive NTFS ACL.
For a folder such as [ICODE]D:\TeamFiles[/ICODE], create or review the SMB share in [B]Computer Management > Shared Folders > Shares[/B], or through the folder’s [B]Sharing[/B] tab. At the share layer, grant the local group the appropriate access—typically Change for contributors or Read for viewers. At the Security tab, grant the same group the corresponding NTFS permission, usually Modify for contributors.
PowerShell can add an allow entry to an existing SMB share:
[CODE]Grant-SmbShareAccess -Name 'TeamFiles' `
  -AccountName "$env:COMPUTERNAME\ProjectEditors" `
  -AccessRight Change -Force[/CODE]
Microsoft’s SMB documentation defines [ICODE]Grant-SmbShareAccess[/ICODE] as adding an allow access-control entry to an SMB share. Check the existing share rules first with [ICODE]Get-SmbShareAccess -Name 'TeamFiles'[/ICODE]; broad entries such as Everyone may still grant access that defeats the purpose of creating a restricted group.
This local-group approach does not make the share remotely reachable on its own. File and Printer Sharing must be enabled, the Windows Firewall rules must permit the connection for the active network profile, and the connecting user must authenticate with an account Windows can recognize on the host.
[HEADING=1]Use PowerShell when the console is unavailable[/HEADING]
Windows Home users and administrators automating several machines can use the LocalAccounts cmdlets rather than attempting to install an unsupported MMC snap-in. Microsoft documents [ICODE]New-LocalGroup[/ICODE], [ICODE]Add-LocalGroupMember[/ICODE], [ICODE]Get-LocalGroupMember[/ICODE], and [ICODE]Remove-LocalGroupMember[/ICODE] for this work.
Run the following in an elevated [B]64-bit Windows PowerShell[/B] session:
[CODE]New-LocalGroup -Name 'ProjectEditors' `
  -Description 'Users permitted to modify D:\TeamFiles'

Add-LocalGroupMember -Group 'ProjectEditors' `
  -Member "$env:COMPUTERNAME\alex"

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'ProjectEditors'[/CODE]
To remove a departed user later:
[CODE]Remove-LocalGroupMember -Group 'ProjectEditors' `
  -Member "$env:COMPUTERNAME\alex"[/CODE]
Use the computer-qualified account name when possible. Microsoft notes a subtle but consequential behavior on domain-joined systems: if a local account has the same name as a domain identity, an unqualified [ICODE]Add-LocalGroupMember[/ICODE] request can select the domain member instead. Qualification makes the intended identity clear.
The LocalAccounts module has one practical trap: Microsoft says it is unavailable in 32-bit PowerShell on a 64-bit system. If the cmdlets appear missing, launch the normal 64-bit Windows PowerShell executable rather than a 32-bit host. The older built-in fallback remains available from an elevated Command Prompt:
[CODE]net localgroup ProjectEditors /add
net localgroup ProjectEditors COMPUTERNAME\alex /add
net localgroup ProjectEditors[/CODE]
The final check should be operational, not cosmetic: sign in as a non-administrator member of the group, create a test file through the local path and, if applicable, through [ICODE]\\COMPUTERNAME\TeamFiles[/ICODE]. Once that succeeds, future access changes reduce to adding or removing a member from [ICODE]ProjectEditors[/ICODE]—without rewriting permissions across the folder tree for each person.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
[HEADING=1]On This Day: September 7[/HEADING]
[HEADING=1]1701 — Europe forms an anti-French supergroup[/HEADING]
England, the Dutch Republic, and the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I signed the Treaty of The Hague, reviving the Grand Alliance against Louis XIV’s France. The immediate problem was Spain: the death of childless King Charles II had left a vast imperial inheritance up for grabs, and Louis’s grandson Philip of Anjou had landed the Spanish crown. Europe looked at that family arrangement and saw a French power surge wearing a Spanish hat.
The treaty set the stage for the War of the Spanish Succession, a conflict that would redraw diplomatic maps and demonstrate that no single monarch—however glittering his palace or enormous his wig—could casually dominate Europe. It also strengthened the idea of a continental “balance of power,” the enduring principle that international politics works best when no one player gets to flip the board.
The alliance’s members did not agree on every detail, because of course they did not: great powers rarely enter a coalition without bringing a suitcase full of grievances. Still, their shared fear of French expansion proved more useful than their differences, and the treaty helped turn a succession dispute into a globe-spanning struggle.
[HEADING=1]1812 — Napoleon wins the battle and loses the plot[/HEADING]
Near the village of Borodino, west of Moscow, Napoleon’s Grande Armée collided with a Russian force commanded by Mikhail Kutuzov. It was a savage, smoky day of artillery barrages, shattered redoubts, cavalry charges, and appalling losses. By nightfall, the Russians had withdrawn, allowing Napoleon to claim the field.
But Borodino was the kind of victory that comes with a giant invoice. Tens of thousands of soldiers had been killed, wounded, or gone missing, and the French army had spent precious strength it could not replace deep inside hostile territory. Napoleon would enter Moscow a week later, only to find that capturing a city was not the same thing as conquering a country.
The Emperor famously held back his Imperial Guard, his elite reserve, rather than commit it to the final push. Historians have argued ever since about whether that caution cost him a decisive win. Either way, Borodino became Napoleon’s bloodiest day—and a brutal prelude to his catastrophic retreat from Russia.
[HEADING=1]1822 — Brazil cuts the Portuguese cord[/HEADING]
Prince Pedro, heir to Portugal’s throne but resident in Brazil, proclaimed Brazilian independence on the banks of the Ipiranga stream near São Paulo. The dramatic “Cry of Ipiranga” came after Portugal’s legislature sought to pull Brazil back under tighter colonial control. Pedro’s answer was essentially: absolutely not, with a sword reportedly involved for emphasis.
Brazil’s break from Portugal created the Empire of Brazil, with Pedro becoming Emperor Pedro I. Unlike much of Spanish America, which splintered into multiple new republics after independence, Brazil remained one enormous political unit. That relative territorial continuity would become one of the country’s defining features.
There is a delicious dynastic twist here: Brazil’s first emperor was the son of Portugal’s king. The famous painting of Pedro dramatically raising his sword amid a grand entourage is more national mythmaking than eyewitness reportage, but the event’s symbolism was real enough. Nations, like movies, often prefer the heroic wide shot.
[HEADING=1]1892 — Gentleman Jim boxes the old guard into retirement[/HEADING]
James J. “Gentleman Jim” Corbett defeated John L. Sullivan in New Orleans to win the world heavyweight championship, knocking him out in the 21st round. Sullivan had been the hulking superstar of bare-knuckle-era prizefighting; Corbett was quicker, cooler, and trained for the new world of gloves and Marquess of Queensberry rules.
The bout marked a major changing of the guard in boxing. Corbett’s scientific footwork, sharp combinations, and stamina made him a prototype for the modern heavyweight champion, while Sullivan represented the rougher, older spectacle of fists, saloons, and nearly limitless rounds. Boxing had put on gloves—and, at least briefly, a collar.
Sullivan outweighed Corbett and entered as the great favorite, but youth and movement turned the fight into a slow-motion upset. The “Gentleman” had once worked as a bank clerk and an actor, a résumé that sounds less like a heavyweight contender than the lead in a very confident Victorian comedy.
[HEADING=1]1921 — Atlantic City invents a crown-shaped tourist trap[/HEADING]
Atlantic City opened the pageant that would become Miss America, hoping to keep visitors spending after Labor Day had emptied the boardwalk. Initially framed as an “Inter-City Beauty” competition, it mixed parades, bathing costumes, promotional hoopla, and the kind of civic ambition that says, “What this resort town needs is more sequins.”
The event grew into one of the most recognizable institutions in American popular culture, shaping—and often reflecting—changing arguments about beauty, gender, celebrity, scholarship, and public performance. For decades, the Miss America title became both a cultural launching pad and a national lightning rod.
The first winner, Margaret Gorman of Washington, D.C., received her top honor on September 8, after the festivities had begun the previous day. She was only 16. The pageant’s founders may have wanted one more weekend of hotel bookings; instead, they accidentally built a century-long debate in a sash.
[HEADING=1]1927 — Philo Farnsworth sends a line into the future[/HEADING]
In a small San Francisco laboratory, 21-year-old inventor Philo T. Farnsworth successfully transmitted an electronic television image: a simple straight line. It was not exactly prestige television. No dragons, no detectives, no cooking competition. But the image was created and scanned electronically, which was the crucial trick.
Farnsworth’s image dissector became a foundation stone for electronic television, the technology that would eventually beam news, sports, sitcoms, moon landings, and late-night advertisements into homes around the world. The screen age began not with a dramatic broadcast, but with a line refusing to stay put on a piece of glass.
Television’s invention was no solo fairy tale. Farnsworth soon faced a bruising patent battle with RCA and rival inventor Vladimir Zworykin. Still, a court recognized Farnsworth’s priority in a key electronic television patent—a rare moment when the young independent inventor managed to land a clean punch on a corporate giant.
[HEADING=1]1936 — Buddy Holly arrives before rock learns to wear glasses[/HEADING]
Charles Hardin Holley—soon known to the world as Buddy Holly—was born in Lubbock, Texas. He would grow into one of rock and roll’s most influential early figures, marrying country twang, rhythm and blues drive, and a songwriter’s instinct for a melody that could jump straight out of the radio.
With the Crickets, Holly helped establish the blueprint for the self-contained rock band: musicians who wrote, arranged, played, and recorded their own songs. “That’ll Be the Day,” “Peggy Sue,” and “Not Fade Away” helped shape the sound of the late 1950s—and sent echoes forward to the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, and beyond.
His career lasted barely 18 months at the top, ending with his death in a plane crash on February 3, 1959, when he was 22. Yet Holly’s influence proved stubbornly immortal. Rock had plenty of swaggering rebels; Holly showed that a shy-looking kid in horn-rimmed glasses could make rebellion sound exquisitely catchy.
[HEADING=1]1940 — London’s long night begins[/HEADING]
Nazi Germany launched its first mass bombing raid on London, beginning the sustained assault remembered as the Blitz. Hundreds of Luftwaffe aircraft struck the city’s docks and surrounding neighborhoods on what became known as Black Saturday. Fires spread along the Thames; civilians were killed in their homes, streets, and shelters.
The raid opened 57 consecutive nights of bombing over London and began an eight-month campaign against British cities. Germany aimed to damage industry, disrupt supply lines, and crush morale. It succeeded in inflicting terrible destruction and civilian suffering, but it failed to force Britain from the war.
Londoners adapted with a grim ingenuity: Underground stations became shelters, blackout curtains became standard domestic equipment, and nightly raids became an awful routine. The Blitz later became central to Britain’s story of wartime endurance, though that story should never obscure the fear, grief, and exhaustion endured beneath the rhetoric.
[HEADING=1]1997 — Mobutu dies, but his wreckage remains[/HEADING]
Mobutu Sese Seko, the former dictator of Zaire, died in exile in Morocco at age 66, only months after rebels had driven him from power. He had ruled the country from 1965, cultivating a personality cult, accumulating immense personal wealth, and turning the state into an engine for patronage, repression, and spectacular corruption.
His fall came amid the First Congo War, led by Laurent-Désiré Kabila and fueled by regional tensions after the Rwandan genocide. Mobutu’s departure ended one man’s 32-year grip on power, but it did not bring peace. The country, renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo, would soon be drawn into another devastating regional war.
Mobutu had renamed the country Zaire as part of his campaign of “Authenticity,” which also encouraged citizens to abandon European names and dress. The man who styled himself as the all-powerful warrior left behind a state so hollowed out that even his grand titles could not hold it together.
[HEADING=1]2008 — Washington grabs the mortgage fire extinguisher[/HEADING]
As the global financial crisis tightened its grip, the U.S. government placed mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into federal conservatorship. The Federal Housing Finance Agency moved to take control, while the Treasury pledged support to keep the firms functioning. The housing market was buckling, and two companies central to American mortgage finance were suddenly too important to fail.
Fannie and Freddie guaranteed or held trillions of dollars in mortgage-related debt, making their survival a matter of systemic financial stability rather than ordinary corporate misfortune. The intervention was one of the defining rescues of the 2008 crisis, intended to preserve the flow of mortgage credit while preventing a far wider panic.
The timing came with a bureaucratic footnote worthy of the crisis itself: the formal conservatorship action was taken on September 6, while the public announcement and Treasury arrangements landed on September 7. Either way, the message was unmistakable—America’s housing-finance system had just acquired a very large federal chaperone.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
The FSP MEGA GM 1200W is a high-capacity ATX 3.1 power supply whose basic proposition is straightforward: provide a modern 1,200 W platform, a native 12V-2x6 graphics cable, and long warranty coverage without relying on an unnamed third-party design. What is less straightforward is its efficiency branding. FSP’s own product listing calls this exact model Gold-rated, yet certification records for the same MEGA-1200GM model document Platinum-level results. That mismatch matters because a power-supply badge is often treated as a simple buying shortcut when the measured reality, test voltage, temperature, and documentation can be more nuanced.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="A modular PC power supply is showcased with performance charts, security shields, and a glowing gaming PC setup."]178309[/ATTACH]
For a Windows PC builder planning a flagship gaming rig, GPU-heavy creator workstation, or compute system, the MEGA GM 1200W has substantial strengths. It also has meaningful caveats: the available evidence does not support one universal full-load efficiency figure, filtering is compliant rather than exceptional, and protection coverage has two specific omissions worth understanding before purchase.
[HEADING=1]The hardware: modern capacity in a compact chassis[/HEADING]
The MEGA-1200GM is a fully modular 1,200 W ATX12V v3.1 PSU measuring 150 × 150 × 86 mm. That 150 mm depth is useful in practical system integration: it should leave more cable-management room than many longer high-wattage units, although a compact case can still become tight once the stiff high-power GPU cable and modular leads are installed.
It uses a single +12 V rail rated at 100 A. In ordinary terms, this means the supply’s primary power budget is not divided among multiple labeled +12 V rails. That can simplify planning for a PC with a high-draw graphics card and modern CPU, but it does not remove the need for sound cable installation and sensible component selection.
The connector provision is appropriately focused on contemporary high-end systems:
[LIST]
[*]One native 600 W PCIe 12V-2x6 cable for current-generation graphics cards.
[*]Two EPS 4+4-pin CPU power cables.
[*]Three conventional PCIe 6+2-pin cables.
[*]Ten SATA and six Molex peripheral connections.
[/LIST]
That is a flexible complement for a workstation with several drives, pumps, fan hubs, or legacy accessories. The pair of EPS cables is particularly helpful for motherboards that use two CPU power inputs. Still, users should connect the native 12V-2x6 cable correctly, avoid severe bends near its connector, and fully seat it at the graphics card. A 1,200 W rating does not compensate for a poorly installed high-current connector.
FSP lists a 10-year warranty. Long coverage is valuable for a PSU because it is one of the few components likely to outlast multiple GPU or platform upgrades. A warranty, however, should be viewed alongside retailer support and local availability, especially where the product is not broadly stocked.
[HEADING=1]An FSP-built platform, with reassuring but bounded teardown evidence[/HEADING]
The available technical evidence identifies FSP as the OEM rather than leaving the underlying platform anonymous. The inspected design uses a half-bridge LLC resonant primary stage and DC-DC conversion for the minor rails. That is a familiar modern topology for a quality high-output consumer PSU, designed to support efficient conversion and regulation across varied loads.
An independent inspection of the tested unit also documented Japanese-brand capacitors, including brands such as Nippon Chemi-Con, Rubycon, and Nichicon. This aligns with a quality-focused component strategy and is more useful than a generic marketing statement alone.
There are two boundaries to keep in mind. First, board-level findings from a sample are not a production-wide bill of materials guarantee. FSP promises Japanese bulk capacitors, but the evidence does not establish that every capacitor in every retail lot is identical. Second, soldering quality should not be generalized too aggressively. An early-production sample was reported to have poor soldering, while the reviewer explicitly expected retail samples to be better. Without comparable teardown evidence across later retail units, neither a blanket condemnation nor a blanket all-clear is justified.
[HEADING=1]Gold on the product page, Platinum in certification records[/HEADING]
The MEGA GM 1200W’s certification story is the central complication in assessing its value.
FSP’s live product page lists 80 PLUS Gold, Cybenetics Gold, and Lambda A++ acoustic certification. Yet a published 80 PLUS verification and testing report for the FSP MEGA-1200GM, dated May 5, 2025, identifies the tested model as 80 PLUS Platinum compliant. It records 93.08% efficiency at 50% load and 89.72% at full load. Cybenetics’ certification record for the MEGA GM 1200W likewise reports Platinum efficiency and A++ noise results at both 115 V and 230 V.
That means it is incorrect to say that Cybenetics is the only independent efficiency credential for this model. An 80 PLUS report exists for the exact model name. It also means buyers should resist reducing the PSU to either a Gold or Platinum label without qualification: the manufacturer’s current page and the certification documents conflict.
There is no published explanation in the available material for why FSP’s Gold labeling differs from both the 80 PLUS report and the Cybenetics record. Possible differences involving regional authorization, production lots, marketing choices, or documentation timing would be inference, not established fact. The practical conclusion is simpler: a shopper should verify the box, regional listing, warranty terms, and current product documentation for the exact unit being purchased rather than assuming every label tells the same story.
[HEADING=1]Efficiency is strong, but voltage and methodology matter[/HEADING]
The measured results broadly support the view that the MEGA GM 1200W is an efficient high-wattage PSU. They do not support treating one lab result as the sole definitive number.
Cybenetics reports average efficiency across more than 1,450 load combinations of 90.431% at 115 V and 92.589% at 230 V. Its results illustrate the expected advantage of 230 V input for this kind of power supply. For North American Windows PC owners using 115 V-class mains power, the 115 V result is the more relevant general reference point.
At a 1,200 W load, test results vary. One measurement recorded 87.731% at 115 V. Another reported 91.7% at full load, while the 80 PLUS report recorded 89.72% at 100% load. These are not necessarily contradictory product failures; efficiency changes with input voltage, ambient temperature, load setup, instrumentation, and laboratory methodology.
The real-world consequence is thermal. At 1,200 W DC output, even a few percentage points of efficiency can translate into a substantial difference in heat that must be exhausted from the PSU and case. A user who regularly renders, compiles, simulates, or runs GPU compute workloads near the unit’s maximum rating should prioritize adequate case airflow and avoid interpreting a certification tier as a guarantee of identical behavior under every workload.
For more typical gaming use, where instantaneous demand can be high but sustained system draw is often well below 1,200 W, the PSU has ample headroom. That does not mean 1,200 W is automatically the right choice: a lower-capacity unit may be better value for a system that will never approach this range. The MEGA GM makes the most sense where expansion headroom, a power-hungry GPU, multiple devices, or sustained heavy work gives that capacity a real purpose.
[HEADING=1]Acoustics and electrical output: good results with caveats[/HEADING]
Cybenetics reports exceptionally low average noise output across its broad test sweep: 14.44 dBA at 115 V and 13.05 dBA at 230 V. The PSU uses a 135 mm hydro-dynamic-bearing fan with selectable semi-passive operation, which helps explain why light and moderate loads can remain quiet.
Noise at the top of the power range is less uniform between testing environments. One full-load result measured 35.4 dB(A), while another reported roughly 55.0 dB(A) at 1,200 W in an approximately 45 °C test environment. Those figures should not be read as directly interchangeable. Hot-box testing can reveal a more demanding scenario than a cooler open-bench measurement, and it is the hotter sustained case that is more relevant to a crowded workstation during a long render.
In short, the MEGA GM is likely to be unobtrusive at modest loads, but a buyer who expects continuous near-maximum output should plan for audible cooling behavior. The surrounding case, intake temperature, and system fan profile will materially affect the result.
Ripple testing also lands in the competent rather than class-leading category. At full load and 115 V, independent results measured 37.4 mV on +12 V, 25.8 mV on +5 V, and 29.8 mV on +3.3 V, all within specification. The same assessment judged the +12 V and +5 V results as not especially competitive and regarded +3.3 V ripple at 115 V as an area that could be improved.
This is not evidence of an out-of-spec unit. It is instead a useful distinction for enthusiasts comparing expensive 1,200 W supplies: passing ripple tests and delivering reliable everyday power are important, but the MEGA GM does not clearly lead every electrical quality metric in its class.
Load regulation tells a similarly nuanced story. Cybenetics measured +12 V, +5 V, and +3.3 V regulation below 1% on its tested sample at 115 V. Another test measured 1.5% on +5 V. The conflict means it is not justified to declare that every MEGA GM fails a claimed ±1% target on the minor rails. It is more accurate to say that results differed by sample or methodology, while neither finding suggests an ordinary PC compatibility concern by itself.
[HEADING=1]Protection coverage has two notable gaps[/HEADING]
Testing confirms functioning over-current, over-power, over-temperature, short-circuit, under-voltage, no-load, and related safeguards in the tested unit. Those are core protections for a premium high-output PSU.
However, the protection set is not complete in every respect. Fan-failure protection is absent, and there is no per-pin over-current protection on the 12V-2x6 connector. The latter does not mean the connector lacks all protection; it means the more granular per-pin safeguard was not present in the tested design.
These omissions deserve more weight in a PSU intended for a high-power GPU than broad phrases such as “full protection suite” imply. They are not, on their own, proof that the unit is unsafe or unsuitable. But a buyer choosing between otherwise comparable models can reasonably prefer a design with fan-failure monitoring and more granular connector protection, particularly for a system regularly operating under sustained load.
Exact OCP and OPP trip figures should also be treated cautiously. Different independent tests reported materially different trigger points, so these should be regarded as sample- and protocol-specific observations rather than fixed retail specifications.
[HEADING=1]Who should consider the MEGA GM 1200W?[/HEADING]
The FSP MEGA GM 1200W is a credible option for users building a high-draw Windows PC who value a compact 1,200 W ATX 3.1 design, two EPS leads, native 12V-2x6 support, an FSP-built platform, and a 10-year warranty. The certification evidence points to strong overall efficiency, including results that meet Platinum thresholds, even though FSP’s own current page calls the product Gold.
The better buying decision is not to assume that the label discrepancy automatically creates a bargain. Compare the actual local price, stock, warranty channel, connector needs, and competing models’ protection features. U.S. availability and a stable street price were not firmly established in the available evidence as of September 7, 2026, despite a reported $229 MSRP and earlier global-launch information.
For a mainstream gaming PC, this supply may be more capacity than necessary. For a flagship GPU system or serious creator workstation, it offers a sound feature set and encouraging test performance, tempered by non-leading ripple results, potentially higher noise under hot full-load conditions, and the two protection omissions. Its most unusual attribute remains the documentation conflict: measured and certified Platinum-level evidence exists, but buyers should purchase based on the exact regional product and its current support terms—not on an unresolved badge dispute alone.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
A recent Fedora-versus-Windows 11 comparison is a useful reminder that an operating system can materially affect how an 8GB laptop feels. It is not, however, proof that Linux is universally faster than Windows. The test’s most striking reported figures—faster and more consistent Fedora booting, far lower apparent memory use after startup, and large advantages in selected creative and development applications—come from a pair of matching Dell XPS 13 laptops. That makes the result relevant to similarly constrained hardware, but it is still one configuration, with important methodological details unavailable.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Two laptops display cosmic and Windows wallpapers in a futuristic city with glowing analytics dashboards."]178308[/ATTACH]
The practical conclusion is narrower and more valuable than the headline argument. On an 8GB machine, a lean Fedora installation may offer a noticeably better experience in some workflows. Windows 11 can also perform very differently depending on the application, game, drivers, power policy, and hardware. Buyers and existing PC owners should treat the comparison as a reason to test their own workloads, not as a final verdict on either platform.
[HEADING=1]What the Dell XPS 13 comparison actually establishes[/HEADING]
The underlying comparison used two identically specified Dell XPS 13 systems: Intel Core 5 320 processors, 8GB of RAM, and 512GB storage. Matching the broad hardware specification is an important starting point. It avoids the most obvious error in cross-platform comparisons, where one operating system is tested on a faster machine than the other.
Reported results favored Fedora in several areas. Fedora was said to boot more consistently, with an average boot result close to half that reported for Windows. The coverage also described a substantial difference in memory shown as in use after startup: roughly 33% for Linux compared with roughly 85% for Windows. Selected applications reportedly showed large Fedora advantages, particularly Visual Studio Code and DaVinci Resolve.
Those observations are meaningful as observations of these two laptops under the conditions of the test. They support the proposition that Fedora can be faster or feel lighter than Windows 11 on an 8GB Dell XPS 13 in particular tasks. That is already a useful finding for people deciding whether an older or entry-level Windows laptop deserves a second life with Linux.
But the same reporting says outcomes changed by workload. Blender did not show the same dramatic separation, although Fedora was still described as slightly faster. This matters because the broad claim—“Linux is faster than Windows”—compresses many unrelated questions into one. Startup behavior, application launch times, CPU rendering, GPU acceleration, file-system performance, browser responsiveness, video editing, and gaming all stress different software layers.
An operating system does not have one permanent speed ranking. The result depends on the application, its build and dependencies, the graphics stack, device drivers, firmware, background activity, storage state, and the power limits selected by the manufacturer or user.
[HEADING=1]Why the 85% versus 33% RAM figure needs care[/HEADING]
The startup-memory figure is the most persuasive-looking number in the comparison, especially to anyone struggling with an 8GB PC. Yet it cannot be read as a simple statement that Windows has left only 15% of the laptop’s RAM usable.
Windows uses otherwise idle memory for cache. Its definition of available memory includes not just completely free memory but also standby memory and pages on the standby list. These are resources Windows can reclaim when an application needs them. Therefore, a high “used” percentage in one view does not necessarily mean that applications will immediately be forced to swap data to storage.
Linux has a similar measurement trap in reverse. Its MemAvailable figure is an estimate of memory that can be allocated to new applications without swapping, rather than a directly interchangeable version of a Windows usage percentage. Both systems attempt to make useful use of RAM, including by caching data that could later be discarded or repurposed.
That does not make the reported difference meaningless. A large post-startup gap may still correlate with a more comfortable multitasking experience on an 8GB device, particularly if a user opens a browser with many tabs, an editor, video tools, and communication software. It is simply not enough on its own to determine how much memory is truly available to the next demanding task.
The more revealing follow-up would be a repeatable workload: open the same browser session, application projects, and media files on both systems; then observe responsiveness, storage paging, and completion time. The available material does not provide such a complete memory-pressure analysis.
[HEADING=1]Why a matched laptop pair is not a complete benchmark[/HEADING]
Hardware matching is necessary, but it is not sufficient for a reproducible operating-system comparison. The accessible evidence does not establish the exact Windows build, Fedora release, kernel, desktop environment, graphics and chipset driver versions, BIOS or firmware revisions, update state, or power settings. It also does not establish that the SSDs were identical models with similar free capacity and storage condition.
Those omissions can matter. Laptop performance may change substantially under a vendor power profile, battery operation, a thermal limit, a driver update, or a difference in whether an application is using a native package, a sandboxed package, or a hardware-accelerated code path. DaVinci Resolve and Blender, for example, can be highly dependent on GPU support and driver behavior. A result in Visual Studio Code can also be affected by extensions, project size, indexing status, and whether caches were warm.
The available reporting also does not document repetitions, raw timings, variance, or error ranges. Without repeated runs, it is difficult to know whether a narrow advantage is reliable or simply ordinary run-to-run variation. A big difference is more likely to be relevant, but even then the cause remains uncertain unless settings and logs are published.
This is not an accusation that the comparison was unfair. It is a limit on what the public evidence can support. The test is best understood as a practical demonstration, not a complete scientific benchmark suite.
[HEADING=1]A separate comparison shows why gaming needs its own answer[/HEADING]
A different 2026 Windows 11-versus-Fedora KDE comparison reinforces the point that results are workload-specific. That test used a much more powerful desktop-class configuration—Ryzen 7 9850X3D processor and Radeon RX 9070 XT graphics—and ran each benchmark three times. It reported Windows ahead in every game tested, while Fedora led by around 3% to 4% in Geekbench and Blender.
This does not invalidate the Dell XPS 13 result. The systems, graphics hardware, and applications are different. Instead, it provides a useful boundary: Linux performance advantages on a low-memory ultrabook do not establish a universal gaming advantage, or even a universal overall advantage.
For Windows users, gaming remains a case where the exact title and graphics configuration should drive the decision. A platform can lead in a compute benchmark yet trail in games because games rely on a distinct mix of graphics drivers, APIs, engine optimizations, anti-cheat compatibility, and vendor tuning. A user whose priority is a particular game should verify that game’s performance and compatibility before replacing Windows.
[HEADING=1]Microsoft’s memory work is relevant, but not an admission of defeat[/HEADING]
Microsoft has publicly said it is working on Windows 11 performance and responsiveness, including memory optimization for PCs with 8GB of RAM and above. That commitment aligns with the everyday concern exposed by the Dell comparison: 8GB remains a constrained amount of memory for a modern desktop system, especially when users multitask.
It would be too strong, though, to portray that work as an acknowledgement that Windows 11 is categorically slow or fundamentally unsuitable for 8GB PCs. Software vendors routinely optimize memory footprint and responsiveness as hardware, applications, and customer expectations evolve. Microsoft’s statement confirms that the company sees optimization as ongoing work; it does not establish a single cause for the results in this comparison.
The important practical implication is that Windows 11 users on 8GB systems should pay attention to future quality and performance updates. Improvements to the platform’s memory footprint could change the balance on the same hardware. Conversely, a Fedora setup is not automatically minimal: the desktop environment, enabled services, browser behavior, and installed applications will determine its real resource demand.
[HEADING=1]What 8GB laptop owners should take from this[/HEADING]
If a Windows 11 laptop becomes unresponsive during ordinary multitasking, the Fedora result gives a credible reason to investigate Linux—particularly for web work, coding, and workflows built around the applications that reportedly favored Fedora. A test installation, where feasible, can answer more than any generalized benchmark: does the laptop support its Wi-Fi, audio, sleep behavior, display controls, peripherals, and the software the owner actually depends on?
Before making a switch, users should identify non-negotiable needs. Windows-only programs, specialized work software, game libraries, enterprise management requirements, and peripherals can outweigh a potential speed gain. The comparison does not establish parity in these areas. It assesses speed in a limited set of tasks, not the whole ownership experience.
Windows users who stay with the platform should avoid interpreting a high idle-memory percentage as a diagnosis by itself. What matters is whether the PC slows under the user’s actual load. A repeatable personal check is more informative: restart the computer, let startup settle, open the same usual applications, and compare responsiveness and task completion after updates or configuration changes. This keeps attention on usable performance rather than a single dashboard reading.
For purchasers, the larger lesson is about memory headroom. The Dell test highlights how exposed an 8GB configuration can be to operating-system overhead and modern multitasking. A system with more memory may reduce the significance of the startup footprint difference, though the available evidence does not quantify how the two operating systems compare at higher capacities.
[HEADING=1]The defensible verdict[/HEADING]
Fedora appears to have delivered compelling advantages in parts of this particular dual-laptop comparison, with the strongest reported signals in boot consistency, apparent post-startup memory use, Visual Studio Code, and DaVinci Resolve. That is enough to challenge the assumption that Windows 11 will always be the fastest or most comfortable option on an 8GB laptop.
It is not enough to declare Linux the winner in every meaningful sense. Some tested workloads differed less, crucial test settings and repetition data are unavailable, and a separate Windows-versus-Fedora comparison found the opposite result in games while giving Fedora only modest leads in selected compute work.
The evidence supports a conditional conclusion: Fedora can be an effective performance-oriented alternative for constrained Windows laptops, but the right operating system remains a workload decision. The more specific the task, hardware, and software stack, the more useful the comparison becomes—and the less credible a universal “faster than” claim is.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
New York City Public Schools’ new AI policy is more selective than the shorthand phrase “AI ban” suggests—and that distinction matters for students, teachers, families, and education-software administrators. For the 2026–27 school year, the system is placing a moratorium on [B]student-facing generative AI[/B] in grades 2K through 8. It is not eliminating every AI-enabled tool, every staff use of AI, or all student exposure to the subject. High schools, meanwhile, will have a constrained mix of AI-literacy instruction and centrally approved use.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="A futuristic classroom contrasts AI caution and innovation against a glowing city skyline."]178307[/ATTACH]
That narrower framing does not make the decision trivial. NYCPS serves a vast number of schools with uneven technology capacity, varied classroom practices, and a substantial inventory of existing software. The policy will require practical changes to what students can access on school-managed devices, which applications teachers can assign, and how schools distinguish an ordinary digital feature from a student-facing generative-AI function. Yet the policy is best understood as a one-year governance test, not as a settled judgment that all AI is unsuitable for education.
[HEADING=1]What NYCPS is restricting[/HEADING]
For 2026–27, software using student-facing generative AI is not permitted for students in grades 2K–8. This is the central rule. It applies to the sort of functionality that generates responses or content for students, rather than to “artificial intelligence” as a broad technological category.
The difference is important because AI is an umbrella term. Describing the policy as a complete prohibition on AI in elementary and middle-school classrooms overstates its scope. The city’s approach includes specified exceptions and permitted uses, including accessibility accommodations. It also does not mean every software product with an AI-related component is necessarily prohibited in every context; the critical policy question is whether students in the covered grades are being given access to generative-AI functionality.
The administration has said it will disable AI components or discontinue use of more than 38 previously allowed programs. That figure illustrates the operational reach of the decision. But the public has not yet received a full list identifying those products. For families and educators, this creates a straightforward but unresolved question: which familiar classroom applications will change, and how will those changes appear in day-to-day lessons?
A school may need to alter assignment workflows, remove a feature from a managed application, or choose a different approved product. For Windows users supporting a school-age child or working in a school, the immediate effect may be less about a new device setting than about changed access within browser-based services and school-installed apps. A tool that remains on a laptop or tablet may have some functions disabled, or it may no longer be available for classroom use.
[HEADING=1]What remains permitted[/HEADING]
The moratorium does not prevent teachers and staff from using approved AI tools for instructional planning and operational work. At the same time, NYCPS places important limits on staff use: approved AI is not to be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or consequential decisions about students.
Those restrictions recognize that a lesson-planning aid and a system that affects a student’s evaluation or treatment are fundamentally different uses. Planning and operational tasks may support staff workflows, while grading and behavior-related decisions can have direct consequences for an individual student. The policy therefore draws a line not only by age group but also by the stakes of a particular use.
This is also a meaningful distinction for school IT teams. Blocking student-facing generative AI is not identical to banning every AI-related software feature from every staff account. In practice, permission controls, account roles, device-management policies, procurement reviews, and vendor settings may all matter. The available information does not spell out a school-level enforcement mechanism, so the consistency of implementation across schools remains an open issue.
That uncertainty should temper assumptions in either direction. It would be premature to conclude the policy will be simple to enforce, but it is equally inaccurate to assume NYCPS has ordered every AI-supported application removed from its systems.
[HEADING=1]High school is a limited-use environment, not an unrestricted one[/HEADING]
The policy treats high school differently. All NYC public high-school students must complete two AI-literacy modules, each 45 minutes long. The city is also allowing five centrally approved educational AI pilots in grades 9–12, alongside limited teacher-supervised use tied to career readiness.
This structure places AI education ahead of broad access. Students are expected to receive formal instruction about the technology, but the policy does not open a general pathway for unrestricted use of generative AI across high-school coursework.
The five-pilot model is particularly notable. A centrally approved pilot can give the system a smaller setting in which to observe implementation before authorizing wider use. But it is not evidence that those programs are effective, safe, equitable, or ready for scale. No outcomes are yet available showing whether the pilots, the literacy modules, or the 2K–8 moratorium will improve learning, student safety, privacy, or equity.
For students, that means access may depend substantially on whether their school participates in an approved pilot or a permitted career-readiness activity. For teachers, it means a lesson that involves generative AI may be allowed in one tightly defined high-school setting while remaining unavailable in a middle-school classroom.
[HEADING=1]A one-year decision with a future review still ahead[/HEADING]
NYCPS has characterized the restriction as a moratorium for the 2026–27 school year. Officials planned to assess the policy before determining what happens afterward. The word “moratorium” is therefore more meaningful than “permanent ban”: the current rule is deliberately time-limited, even if its future direction is unknown.
Several paths remain possible after the assessment. The city could extend the restriction, revise it, end it, or retain the age-based framework while changing the types of permitted tools. None of those outcomes is established today.
The temporary nature of the policy may be useful from a public-administration perspective because it gives NYCPS an opportunity to examine real implementation problems: whether schools can reliably identify covered features, whether approved high-school programs function as intended, and whether teachers have workable alternatives. But a one-year policy also puts pressure on the system to define what it will measure and how it will apply lessons learned. The available policy information does not yet establish those evaluation standards.
[HEADING=1]Why the public debate is split[/HEADING]
The disagreement is not simply between supporters and opponents of AI. It involves competing views about how quickly schools should move, how young students should be when they encounter generative systems, and whether a limited exception model provides enough protection.
A group of 29 New York City Council members urged the mayor and schools chancellor to adopt a two-year moratorium. Their letter argued that draft guidance did not propose stronger student-data privacy protections. That is a significant political intervention, but it should not be described as a formal decision by the City Council as a whole. Available reporting establishes support from 29 members, not a Council-wide vote or enacted measure.
Some advocates who preferred a two-year pause have objected to the high-school pilot exemptions. Their position reflects a concern that limited approved use could undermine the purpose of a broader precautionary approach.
On the other side, Richard Buery publicly opposed a blanket one-year restriction through middle school. That view holds that a broad age-based pause may be too blunt an instrument. The competing arguments reveal a real policy tension: a system can restrict student access to reduce potential risk, but it may also delay experience with tools that are increasingly relevant to future education and work.
Neither position, by itself, proves what the policy will achieve. There is not yet outcome evidence demonstrating that a longer pause, a one-year moratorium, high-school pilots, or earlier access produces the best results. The dispute is about risk management and educational judgment under uncertainty.
[HEADING=1]The implementation questions that matter most[/HEADING]
The policy’s success will depend less on its headline than on answers to several unresolved operational questions.
First, schools, educators, and families need clarity about the more than 38 affected programs. Without a published product list, it is difficult to know which services have changed, whether a feature has been disabled instead of the whole program removed, and what replacement workflow is expected.
Second, school-level enforcement has not been clearly specified. A central policy is one thing; preventing unapproved student-facing use across many classrooms, accounts, and products is another. This is especially relevant where software settings differ between student and staff accounts or where a product updates its feature set over time.
