Third, the city must make the high-school boundaries understandable. Students and teachers need to know what is covered by the required literacy modules, what the five pilots permit, and how the career-readiness exception operates under teacher supervision. Vague boundaries can yield uneven access or cautious overcompliance, where educators avoid even permitted activities because they cannot tell what is allowed.
Finally, the eventual assessment needs to distinguish technical compliance from educational results. Disabling a feature can show that a restriction was implemented. It cannot alone show whether students learned more, whether staff workflows improved, or whether the policy affected equity between schools. Those are separate questions.
[HEADING=1]What families, educators, and IT staff should watch[/HEADING]
Families should expect the practical effects to vary by grade. Younger students and middle-school students should not be assigned software that gives them student-facing generative-AI access under the moratorium. High-school families may instead see AI-literacy activities and, at some schools, narrowly approved pilot experiences.
Teachers should separate permitted staff use from student use. An approved tool used for planning does not automatically make it appropriate for students, and it cannot be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or consequential student decisions. When a tool’s status is unclear, the sensible question is not merely whether it is labeled “AI,” but whether it provides generative functionality to students in the covered grades and whether the use is authorized.
For technology administrators, the policy makes application governance a central issue. The missing list of affected programs and the absence of a fully described school-level enforcement process mean administrators will need clear district direction before they can confidently align device images, app catalogs, identity permissions, browser access, and staff guidance. On Windows PCs, as on other school-managed devices, the policy challenge is likely to center on software access and account configuration rather than the operating system itself.
NYCPS has chosen a middle course: a strong temporary restriction for younger students, controlled exposure and instruction in high school, and limited staff use subject to consequential safeguards. Whether that becomes a durable model will depend on what the city learns during 2026–27—and on whether it supplies the implementation clarity that schools need to make the rules consistent in practice.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
A proxy error in Windows 10 or Windows 11 can survive a perfectly working Wi-Fi connection because Windows keeps more than one proxy path. The Settings app controls the signed-in user’s web proxy configuration, while [B]WinHTTP[/B] maintains a separate machine-level configuration used by many Windows components and services. Microsoft’s Support guidance places the visible controls under Settings > Network & internet > Proxy; Microsoft Learn separately documents [ICODE]netsh winhttp[/ICODE] for the system configuration.
That split explains a common pattern: Edge or another browser opens sites after a proxy change, but Windows Update, Microsoft Store downloads, activation, an endpoint-security agent, or a background service still cannot reach the internet. Do not begin by resetting the whole network stack. First establish whether the failure is caused by a stray manual proxy, a broken automatic-configuration script, an obsolete WinHTTP setting, or an organization policy that will simply put the setting back.
[HEADING=1][ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Windows proxy settings and terminal output illustrate browser and service traffic routed through a corporate proxy."]178305[/ATTACH]Start with the Windows proxy page[/HEADING]
Open [B]Settings > Network & internet > Proxy[/B]. The labels vary slightly between Windows 10 and Windows 11, but the three relevant methods are the same: automatic detection, a setup script, and a manual proxy server.
For a personally owned PC on a typical home connection, the usual healthy state is:
[LIST]
[*]“Automatically detect settings” can remain on if it has not caused a repeatable delay or failure on the current network.
[*]“Use setup script” should be off unless you were given a specific PAC-script address by an employer, school, hotel, or network operator.
[*]“Use a proxy server” should be off unless you intentionally use a proxy and know its server name and port.
[/LIST]
A manual proxy left behind by old VPN software, a browser privacy tool, malware, or a previous workplace is the simplest failure to correct. Select [B]Set up[/B] beside “Use a proxy server,” turn it off, save the change, close and reopen the affected browser or app, and test a normal HTTPS site.
Do not casually remove a setup-script address on a managed work device. A PAC file—short for [I]Proxy Auto-Configuration[/I]—can send traffic directly for some destinations and through a required proxy for others. Deleting it may make ordinary browsing appear healthier while breaking access to company applications, internal sites, or security controls.
Microsoft’s own proxy documentation also makes an important limitation clear: a VPN connection that uses a proxy must be configured separately for that VPN. If the error occurs only after connecting to a corporate VPN, changing the general Windows proxy page may be beside the point. Disconnect the VPN and repeat the test before treating the local PC as the cause.
[HR][/HR]
[HEADING=1]Check the setting that background services actually use[/HEADING]
The Proxy page is not the complete picture. Microsoft’s Windows Update documentation says the update client uses WinHTTP to scan for updates, while BITS and Delivery Optimization handle downloads. Microsoft also documents that Internet Explorer-era user proxy settings—now surfaced through Windows Settings—are not necessarily the same as WinHTTP’s system-level setting.
Open [B]Windows Terminal (Admin)[/B], Command Prompt as administrator, or PowerShell as administrator. Then run:
[ICODE]netsh winhttp show proxy[/ICODE]
There are two broad results:
[ICODE]Direct access (no proxy server).[/ICODE]
or a configured proxy server and, potentially, a bypass list. “Direct access” means WinHTTP has no static proxy configured. It does [B]not[/B] prove every application is using direct access, nor does it rule out automatic discovery, application-specific proxy rules, VPN behavior, DNS failures, a firewall, or a captive portal.
If [ICODE]show proxy[/ICODE] displays an old proxy host, a proxy address that no longer resolves, or a server you do not recognize on a personal machine, preserve the result before changing it. The command below can save the current WinHTTP configuration as a script-like record:
[ICODE]netsh winhttp dump[/ICODE]
Copy the output into a text file along with the date, the network name, and whether a VPN was connected. This small step makes a reset reversible in practice: it gives an IT administrator something concrete to compare with the intended configuration instead of a vague report that “the internet stopped working.”
If the device is personally owned and should use no proxy, reset the static WinHTTP proxy:
[ICODE]netsh winhttp reset proxy[/ICODE]
Microsoft documents that this resets the WinHTTP proxy setting to [ICODE]DIRECT[/ICODE]. Run [ICODE]netsh winhttp show proxy[/ICODE] again to confirm that result, then retry the affected service. A restart is usually unnecessary, although closing and reopening the affected application—or restarting a service that remains stuck—may be needed before it makes a new request.
[B]This command is a configuration change, not a universal repair.[/B] On a corporate network that requires an outbound proxy, [ICODE]reset proxy[/ICODE] can stop Windows Update, management agents, and other Local System services from reaching the internet. Restore the intended proxy only with values supplied by the organization, rather than guessing at a hostname and port.
[HEADING=1]Use the symptom split to avoid the wrong repair[/HEADING]
A browser failure and a Windows-service failure can look identical—“cannot connect to proxy server”—while coming from different configurations. The useful diagnostic question is [I]which clients fail under which account and network condition[/I].
If browsers and desktop applications fail together, begin with the Proxy page. A manual proxy toggle or PAC script may be intercepting the signed-in user’s web traffic. If Windows Update, Store downloads, device-management tools, or scheduled services fail while browsing succeeds, inspect WinHTTP before changing browser settings again.
Microsoft’s Windows Update troubleshooting material specifically warns that a user-level proxy can be configured while WinHTTP remains unconfigured, producing update connectivity failures. In a network that genuinely requires a proxy, the remedy may be to import the working user proxy configuration into WinHTTP:
[ICODE]netsh winhttp import proxy source=ie[/ICODE]
Despite the command’s [ICODE]ie[/ICODE] name, Microsoft still uses it to refer to the legacy WinINet configuration that Windows exposes through proxy settings. Importing is appropriate only after confirming that the user-side proxy setting is the approved one. It copies a configuration; it does not validate that the proxy server is live, that its authentication method works for Local System, or that a PAC file is suitable for every service.
For organizations that use a fixed proxy for devices, the intended configuration may instead be set explicitly by administrators with [ICODE]netsh winhttp set proxy[/ICODE] or through management tooling. Microsoft cautions in its Delivery Optimization documentation that setting a device-wide static WinHTTP proxy affects all user contexts and background services. That is why a workstation fix should not turn into an unplanned fleet configuration.
[HR][/HR]
[HEADING=1]Clear automatic-discovery state only when it is the suspected fault[/HEADING]
Automatic detection relies on WPAD, the Web Proxy Auto-Discovery Protocol, and a network may also provide a PAC file. These mechanisms are useful in managed environments, but a network change can leave clients trying a stale discovery result or inaccessible script.
If “Automatically detect settings” is enabled and the problem began after moving between office, home, hotel, guest Wi-Fi, or VPN networks, reset the WinHTTP auto-proxy state from an elevated terminal:
[ICODE]netsh winhttp reset autoproxy[/ICODE]
Then retry on the same network. Microsoft describes this reset as clearing the WinHTTP proxy auto-discovery service’s settings or cache. It is more targeted than wiping the static WinHTTP proxy configuration, so it is the better first command when the device must retain a known corporate proxy but automatic discovery appears to be the immediate problem.
Do not repeatedly run the command and assume every invocation had an effect. Microsoft’s WinHTTP API documentation notes a timing limitation for repeated auto-proxy resets. More importantly, a reset cannot repair a broken PAC URL, missing WPAD DNS/DHCP configuration, proxy authentication requirement, or an upstream proxy outage. If a setup script is present, record its address and hand that detail to the network administrator.
[HEADING=1]Determine whether work or school management owns the setting[/HEADING]
Before treating a stubborn proxy as corruption, check whether the computer is managed. Open [B]Settings > Accounts > Access work or school[/B]. A listed work or school connection is evidence that an organization can manage the device, although its presence alone does not prove it controls proxy configuration.
For a stronger local check, run the following from a regular Command Prompt:
[ICODE]dsregcmd /status[/ICODE]
Look for Azure AD, domain-join, and MDM enrollment information in the output. On a domain-connected PC, an administrator can also generate a Group Policy Result report:
[ICODE]gpresult /h "%USERPROFILE%\Desktop\gpresult.html"[/ICODE]
Open the resulting HTML report and inspect the applied User and Computer policies for Internet settings, browser policies, or Settings-page restrictions. Microsoft documents that Group Policy can hide the Proxy page itself, including through the [ICODE]network-proxy[/ICODE] Settings-page identifier. It also documents that Group Policy Preferences can reapply a preferred configuration at the next policy refresh even if a user manually changes it.
That behavior produces a clear diagnostic result: if a proxy returns after you turn it off, or the control is grayed out, unavailable, or disappears, stop resetting it. Record the proxy server, PAC-script address, output of [ICODE]netsh winhttp show proxy[/ICODE], device enrollment status, and the exact time the setting reverted. The fix belongs with the organization’s IT team, which can identify whether Group Policy, MDM, VPN software, a secure web gateway agent, or a login script owns the setting.
On a personal device, a proxy that repeatedly re-enables without an identifiable management connection warrants a security check. Review recently installed VPNs, “web protection” suites, browser proxy extensions, and remote-access tools; then run a full scan with Microsoft Defender or the organization’s approved endpoint security product. Resetting the toggle without finding the program or policy that changes it only masks the cause.
The practical endpoint is simple: use the Settings page to repair the signed-in user’s proxy path, use [ICODE]netsh winhttp show proxy[/ICODE] to inspect the service path, and reset only the path that is wrong. When a managed device restores the proxy, the repeatable evidence is more valuable than another reset—and it gives the administrator exactly what is needed to correct the enforced configuration.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
A cleaner Windows 11 taskbar is a realistic goal, but it helps to separate decluttering from disabling. Removing a button can make the desktop calmer without removing the underlying feature, while several similarly named Search and Start options govern entirely different kinds of content. Treating all of them as one “debloat” switch leads to surprises: a hidden Widgets button can still leave the Widgets board available, and turning off Search highlights is not the same as stopping web results.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Futuristic Windows-style interface with glowing icons, toggles, devices, and a central blue abstract logo."]178303[/ATTACH]
The most dependable approach is to first decide what you want less of: taskbar chrome, proactive content, cross-device prompts, or online search integration. Then use the matching supported control and verify the result on your own Windows 11 build. That matters especially now, because Start customization is evolving and some newer controls were first announced for Insider testing rather than as universal retail features.
[HEADING=1]Start with the taskbar buttons[/HEADING]
Windows 11 officially allows the Search display, Task View button, and Widgets button to be hidden from the taskbar. For people who prefer a compact row of pinned applications, this is the lowest-risk cleanup: it removes visual entry points but preserves familiar alternative ways to reach the features.
That distinction is especially useful for Task View. Hiding its taskbar button does not take away virtual desktops or the window-switching interface. [B]Win+Tab[/B] continues to open Task View, so users who only occasionally organize windows or move work between desktops can reclaim taskbar space without giving up the capability.
Search works much the same way. A desktop Search box or button is not necessary if your normal habit is pressing the Windows key and typing, or using [B]Win+S[/B]. Removing the taskbar Search display therefore makes sense for keyboard-first users and for anyone who considers the field redundant beside Start search.
Widgets are the area where a hidden button is most often mistaken for a disabled feature. Windows documents that the Widgets board remains accessible with [B]Win+W[/B] or an edge swipe even after the Widgets button is removed. In other words, this setting primarily removes the persistent taskbar affordance. It is a good compromise for someone who rarely checks Widgets but wants the board on demand.
The implication is simple: if the goal is fewer buttons, hide them. If the goal is to prevent a feature from being opened or to limit its information flow, a button toggle alone is not enough evidence that either outcome has occurred.
[HEADING=1]Widgets: reduce prominence, but understand what remains[/HEADING]
Widgets can surface personalized Discover news content as well as weather, announcements, and notification badges on the taskbar. That can be useful at a glance, but it can also make the taskbar feel more like a stream of changing content than a launcher.
Removing the Widgets button eliminates one prominent route into that experience. It may be all that is needed for a user whose concern is distraction from the taskbar. But because [B]Win+W[/B] remains available, it should not be described as an uninstall or a complete shutdown of Widgets.
This difference also cautions against broad performance claims. Widgets contain dynamic content, but the available evidence does not establish that hiding the button—or changing related taskbar and Start settings—measurably makes Start or the taskbar load faster, including on slow internet connections. A machine may feel quieter after fewer dynamic elements are visible, which is a valid preference. It is not the same as a demonstrated latency or network-use improvement.
[HEADING=1]Cross-device Resume is not a standard taskbar item for everyone[/HEADING]
Windows 11’s Cross-device Resume feature deserves a separate decision rather than being grouped automatically with Widgets and Task View. It is intended to continue a supported activity between a linked Android device and a PC through a taskbar alert.
It also has significant prerequisites: Windows 11, an Android 10 or later device, internet connectivity, Link to Windows, Mobile devices setup, and a supported activity or app. Microsoft’s listed support as of January 2026 includes Spotify, vivo Browser, and WhatsApp. Consequently, it is not a generic taskbar item that every fresh Windows 11 installation will show or use.
For people who do not link an Android phone to Windows, Resume may have little practical relevance. For those who do, it could be helpful rather than clutter: a taskbar alert can save time when transferring a listening session, browser activity, or supported conversation flow from phone to PC.
There is an important settings ambiguity to keep in mind. Independent reporting describes a Resume toggle under [B]Settings > Personalization > Taskbar[/B], while Microsoft’s consumer guidance directs users who want the feature off to [B]Settings > Apps > Resume[/B]. The supplied material does not establish whether a taskbar-level option merely hides the alert or fully disables the underlying cross-device feature. A user seeking to stop Resume itself should follow the consumer-facing Resume setting, then test whether activity-transfer prompts cease. A user who only wants a less busy taskbar should be careful not to assume that hiding an entry has the same effect.
[HEADING=1]Search has three different decluttering problems[/HEADING]
Windows Search attracts more confusion than any other part of this cleanup because three separate changes are frequently conflated.
[HEADING=2]1. Hiding the Search button or box[/HEADING]
This is the taskbar-layout choice described above. It removes the visible Search launch point; it does not stop Start typing or [B]Win+S[/B], and it does not by itself define what appears in search results.
[HEADING=2]2. Turning off Search highlights[/HEADING]
Search highlights are content in Search home and the Start-menu search box. Windows has a documented policy setting, [B]AllowSearchHighlights[/B], whose disabled state turns off those highlights in Windows 11.
This can be a sensible option for users who want Search to feel more like a direct tool for files, settings, and apps rather than a surface for changing featured material. However, it is not a documented switch for eliminating Bing or all web-based results. Anyone expecting that outcome should not rely on the highlights setting alone.
[HEADING=2]3. Blocking web queries and web results[/HEADING]
This is the more consequential Search configuration, and it is not equivalent to hiding Search or disabling highlights. Microsoft documents a policy route that uses two values under the Windows Search policy path: [B]DisableWebSearch=1[/B] and [B]ConnectedSearchUseWeb=0[/B].
That documentation is provided in guidance for Windows 10/11 Server and Enterprise editions. It should therefore not be portrayed as a universal, consumer-friendly Windows 11 tweak. Availability, management policy, edition, and the effects on a particular build all need testing. On a managed work PC, changing administrative Search policies may also conflict with organizational configuration; users should not alter those settings without permission from their IT administrator.
A commonly circulated alternative uses the per-user Explorer policy value [B]DisableSearchBoxSuggestions[/B] set to 1 and then restarts Windows. The available documentation for that exact instruction is a Microsoft Q&A community answer from 2022, not current product documentation. More importantly, it is a different key from Microsoft’s documented web-search policy values. That means it cannot be responsibly advertised as a guaranteed modern solution for removing every Bing suggestion, weather card, memory, or web result.
For most home users, the practical order is safer than jumping directly into Registry Editor: first hide the taskbar Search display if it is unwanted, then disable Search highlights if changing featured Search content is the goal. Only investigate policy-based web-result controls when the Windows edition and build support them, the trade-offs are understood, and a restore point or backup is available. Registry and policy changes can be harder to diagnose later than ordinary Settings changes.
[HEADING=1]Start recommendations: manage expectations by build and channel[/HEADING]
Windows 11 Start includes settings for recently added apps, most-used apps, recently opened items, and folders near the power button. These controls provide useful ways to limit the amount of history and suggestion-like material visible in Start. Microsoft’s Windows 11 settings reference also identifies a setting for Start recommendations.
What they do not guarantee is a single, universal Start layout. It is unsafe to promise that the Recommended area will always remain after recommendation-related settings are changed—or that it will always disappear. In May 2026, Microsoft announced section-level controls for Experimental-channel Insiders that would independently show or hide the Pinned, Recommended, and All sections in Start.
That announcement is encouraging for users who want a more deliberate Start design, but it is not proof that every retail Windows 11 PC has those controls. Feature rollouts are staged, and Insider-channel features can differ from the stable build installed on a household or business PC. If a guide or screenshot shows direct controls to hide an entire Start section and you cannot find them, the likely explanation may be build availability rather than user error.
A reasonable current strategy is to turn off the specific recent and most-used content you do not want, configure power-adjacent folders to match your workflow, and then inspect Start after the change. If your build offers independent section visibility controls, use them deliberately. If it does not, avoid unsupported workarounds simply to force a particular layout.
[HEADING=1]A practical cleanup order[/HEADING]
For a minimal-risk Windows 11 reset, begin with reversible Settings changes:
[LIST=1]
[*]Hide the Search display, Task View button, and Widgets button if they duplicate keyboard shortcuts or add visual noise.
[*]Keep [B]Win+S[/B], [B]Win+Tab[/B], and [B]Win+W[/B] in mind so the hidden features remain easy to reach when genuinely useful.
[*]Decide whether Widgets are merely too prominent or whether their changing content is itself unwanted; hiding the button addresses the former, not necessarily the latter.
[*]Review Resume only if you use a linked Android phone. Disable the feature through its dedicated Resume setting if the aim is to stop cross-device continuation, rather than assuming a taskbar control does that.
[*]Turn off Search highlights if you want less featured content in Search, while recognizing that this is separate from web-result policy.
[*]Reduce Start’s recently added, most-used, and recent-item content, then check whether your particular build offers section-level Start controls.
[/LIST]
The result should be judged by usability, not ideology. A sparse taskbar can reduce distraction and leave more room for application buttons. Yet Task View, Widgets, Search, and Resume each solve legitimate problems for some people. Windows 11’s best decluttering tools are the ones that let you lower their visibility without confusing that choice with a claim that they have been removed, blocked, or made faster.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
Windows 11’s Android integration is more useful when it is treated as a set of separate tools rather than one seamless “phone on your PC” feature. Phone Link can handle messages, notifications, calls, and—in supported cases—mobile apps. File Explorer can now expose a linked Android device’s files wirelessly. A linked phone can also serve as a webcam. And some PCs will show a companion panel in Start.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="A laptop and smartphone showcase interconnected communication, media, and productivity apps in a neon-lit workspace."]178302[/ATTACH]
That breadth can reduce the number of times you need to unlock a phone during the workday, but the experience is uneven by design. The dependable features are not necessarily the flashy ones, and compatibility depends on the particular task, the phone model, Android version, Link to Windows version, network, and sometimes market. The practical way to approach it is to enable the capabilities that solve a specific desktop problem, then treat app streaming and advanced clipboard sharing as optional bonuses.
[HEADING=1]Think in three separate Windows experiences[/HEADING]
The first and most familiar route is [B]Phone Link[/B], paired with the Link to Windows app on Android. Microsoft positions it as the place to read and reply to text messages, see notifications, make and receive calls, access recent photos, and use selected mobile-app features. For routine communication, this is the core experience.
The second route is [B]Windows 11’s Mobile devices integration[/B]. This is where the connected-camera feature is enabled, and it is also relevant to the newer File Explorer connection. It is not simply another tab inside Phone Link. In particular, Windows 11’s photo experience is moving away from Phone Link’s former Photos tab and into File Explorer.
The third is the [B]Mobile device companion in the Start menu[/B]. Where it is available, the panel can show Android battery and connectivity status and offer paths to Messages, Calls, Photos, recent activities, and sending files. It is useful as a quick status and launch surface, not a prerequisite for the rest of the integration. Microsoft describes this as a gradual rollout, so readers should not assume that the panel will appear on every Windows 11 installation immediately.
Separating these paths avoids a common setup mistake: looking for every phone-related feature in Phone Link. It also helps explain why one capability may be present while another is missing.
[HEADING=1]Start with the high-value, broadly useful features[/HEADING]
For many Windows users, the most practical Phone Link functions are messages, notifications, and calls. Keeping text conversations on the larger screen can be genuinely helpful when a response requires copying a tracking number, an address, or a meeting detail into a desktop application. Notifications are similarly useful when they are managed deliberately rather than mirrored indiscriminately.
Calls have a clear technical requirement that is easy to overlook: Phone Link needs a Bluetooth connection between the Windows PC and Android phone to place or receive calls through the PC. Microsoft’s stated baseline is a Bluetooth-capable PC, Android 10 or later, and either Windows 11 or Windows 10 version 1903 (the May 2019 Update) or later. In other words, calling is not exclusive to Windows 11, even though newer Windows 11 integrations are.
A sensible work configuration is to allow only the notification categories that warrant interruption—perhaps direct messages and calendar-related alerts—and turn off noisier app notifications. The goal is not to reproduce a phone’s lock screen on a desktop. It is to let the PC handle small, actionable interactions without creating a second stream of distractions.
There is an important privacy trade-off. Message permissions can expose sensitive content in Phone Link, including two-factor authentication text messages. That can be acceptable on a personally controlled PC with a locked Windows account, but it deserves more caution on a shared household computer, a public-facing workstation, or any device that other people can access while you are signed in.
[HEADING=1]File Explorer is now the better place for Android photos and files[/HEADING]
The most consequential recent change is that linked Android photos are moving into Windows 11 File Explorer rather than remaining centered in Phone Link’s Photos tab. This is more than a cosmetic relocation. File Explorer is designed for file work, and the phone connection can expose folders beyond the camera roll.
On a compatible setup, Windows 11 can wirelessly browse and manage files stored on the Android phone. The available actions include opening, copying, moving, renaming, and deleting files, as well as transferring files between the phone and PC. That makes the feature more useful than a “recent photos” viewer: it can become a direct route for bringing a document, recording, download, or image into a Windows workflow without hunting for a cable.
Microsoft’s documented requirements for this File Explorer capability are Windows 11, Android 11 or later, and Link to Windows version 1.24072.258.0 or later. Those are the thresholds to check before concluding that the feature is unavailable.
This point also corrects an outdated assumption about compatibility. File Explorer access is not documented as a Samsung-, HONOR-, or OnePlus-only privilege tied to a particular Android skin. The published requirements are based on Windows 11, Android version, and Link to Windows version. That is a different and broader eligibility model from app streaming, which remains heavily device-dependent.
For users who regularly import phone-shot images, this matters. Rather than treating Phone Link as the destination for photos, look for the linked phone in File Explorer and work with its folders as part of the normal desktop file-management process. Be careful with destructive operations: the documented feature includes deletion and moving, so actions performed from the PC can alter the phone’s stored files.
[HEADING=1]A phone can be a Windows webcam—if it meets the threshold[/HEADING]
Windows 11 can use a linked Android phone’s camera as a webcam in PC applications. For a laptop with an aging built-in camera, or a desktop without a strong webcam, that can be a meaningful option because a modern phone camera may be the better piece of hardware already on hand.
The documented requirements are specific: the PC must run Windows 11 or later, the Android phone must run Android 10 or later, and Link to Windows must be version 1.24022.0 or later. The setting is enabled through [B]Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Mobile devices > Manage devices[/B].
This should be understood as a Windows linked-device feature. The available documentation establishes the requirements and the Windows setting, but does not substantiate broader claims about the underlying architecture or whether it is “inside” Phone Link. For users, that distinction is less important than knowing where to enable it and why it may be absent on an older phone or outdated app installation.
Before relying on the phone for an important meeting, test it in the actual PC application you use. The documentation confirms that it can be used as a webcam in PC apps, but an individual setup can still vary based on software versions, permissions, and the application’s own device-selection behavior.
[HEADING=1]App streaming is the least universal feature[/HEADING]
The Phone Link Apps and Phone screen features create the most compelling screenshots, but they have the strongest limitations. They should not be described as a general right available to every Android phone.
Microsoft’s supported-device material identifies selected Samsung, HONOR, OPPO, ASUS, OnePlus, Realme, vivo, iQOO, Xiaomi, and ROG devices, with capabilities varying by model, software, feature, and market. Android version availability itself can depend on the device, carrier, and region. Google Pixel does not appear on the official Apps compatibility list, although that absence alone does not establish why it is absent.
Even on a supported device, Phone screen depends on both the PC and phone being connected to the same Wi-Fi network. That requirement has real workplace consequences. Enterprise networks, public Wi-Fi, and VPN arrangements can interfere with the experience, so a feature that works at home should not automatically be expected to work on a managed office network.
There are also functional boundaries:
[LIST]
[*]Only apps in the Android device’s default profile appear in Phone Link. Work and other Android profiles are excluded.
[*]Some Android apps block casting to another screen.
[*]Some apps may fail to work or may display a black screen.
[*]Sound from the Android app continues playing on the phone rather than automatically moving to the PC.
[/LIST]
Those limitations make app streaming best suited to occasional, compatible tasks rather than as a replacement for native Windows software. If it works with a personal messaging app, a smart-home controller, or a utility that lacks a good desktop client, it may be convenient. For work apps, media playback, protected-content apps, or anything dependent on a managed profile, expectations should be conservative.
[HEADING=1]Clipboard sharing is useful, but narrow[/HEADING]
Cross-device copy and paste has similar compatibility constraints. It is supported on Surface Duo and selected devices from Samsung, HONOR, OPPO and OnePlus, ASUS, vivo, and Xiaomi. Its current content scope is limited to text and images; it is not a general-purpose way to move arbitrary file types through the clipboard. Images over 1 MB are resized.
That makes it handy for pasting a short note, a code fragment, a URL, or a small image into a Windows app. It is a poor choice for preserving a full-resolution image or transferring a file where exact fidelity matters. File Explorer’s wireless phone access is the more appropriate route for files on compatible Windows 11 and Android 11-plus devices.
[HEADING=1]A practical setup and troubleshooting order[/HEADING]
The fastest way to avoid disappointment is to validate each goal separately:
[LIST=1]
[*][B]Pair the Android phone and PC for Phone Link[/B], then verify basic messages and notifications first. These are the features most likely to justify the connection day to day.
[*][B]For calls, verify Bluetooth[/B], not merely Wi-Fi. Confirm that the PC supports Bluetooth and that the phone meets the Android 10 baseline.
[*][B]For files and photos, check Windows 11, Android 11, and Link to Windows version 1.24072.258.0 or newer.[/B] Then use File Explorer rather than relying on an older instruction that points to the Phone Link Photos tab.
[*][B]For the phone-camera webcam option, check the lower Android 10 baseline and Link to Windows version 1.24022.0 or newer[/B], then enable it in Mobile devices settings.
[*][B]For Apps or Phone screen, consult the model-specific compatibility situation before troubleshooting.[/B] If the phone is not among the supported families or the feature is not available in the market, repeated re-pairing is unlikely to solve it.
[*][B]When app streaming fails, test the network and the app itself.[/B] Both devices need the same Wi-Fi network, and an individual Android app may deliberately block casting or otherwise refuse to run.
[/LIST]
This sequence distinguishes a missing requirement from a genuine fault. It also keeps users from granting extensive permissions or changing network settings for an advanced feature that their device is not eligible to use.
[HEADING=1]The realistic Windows 11 payoff[/HEADING]
Phone Link is most convincing when it reduces small points of friction: replying to a text without picking up the phone, answering a call through a PC headset, retrieving a phone file in File Explorer, or using the phone camera for a video call. These are concrete integrations with clear requirements.
It is less convincing as a promise that every Android app, every clipboard item, every photo workflow, and every Start-menu panel will behave identically across Android hardware. Microsoft’s own compatibility boundaries make that clear. The right expectation is a capable but modular bridge between Windows and Android: start with communications and File Explorer, add camera support if needed, and regard streamed apps as a model- and network-dependent extra rather than the foundation of the experience.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
Switzerland’s federal government is not removing Microsoft 365 from 3,000 computers. What it has announced is more measured, but strategically significant: a CHF 9 million first-phase program to make a separate “sovereign workplace” with core office functions available to roughly 3,000 selected federal employees from the end of 2027.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="A Swiss cybersecurity command center overlooks alpine peaks, with digital maps, servers, and cloud security displays."]178296[/ATTACH]
The distinction matters for Windows users, IT administrators, and policymakers. The new environment is intended to run [B]in parallel[/B] with Microsoft 365, not replace it immediately. Federal officials have left open the possibility of a later, more complete sovereign workplace, but that remains a question for the program to examine and decide rather than an approved migration outcome.
[HEADING=1]What Switzerland has actually approved[/HEADING]
The Federal Chancellery announced the follow-on program on September 2, 2026, after its proof-of-concept work under the BOSS project. The target is availability of a sovereign workplace solution for around 3,000 selected users by the end of 2027. The Chancellery estimates CHF 9 million for this first phase.
That is a platform-building and operational-testing commitment, not a final decision to displace Microsoft 365 throughout the federal administration. The official design is explicit: the sovereign workplace should be an independent solution operating alongside Microsoft 365.
This wording rules out several easy but misleading interpretations:
[LIST]
[*]It is not a confirmed removal of Microsoft software from 3,000 physical PCs.
[*]It is not a commitment to migrate all federal workers.
[*]It is not a declaration that the 3,000-user environment will become the default federal desktop in 2027.
[*]It is not yet evidence that the program will lower total IT costs.
[/LIST]
The end-of-2027 date is an availability target for selected users, not a confirmed deadline for a broad migration. The Chancellery has also said that any large-scale introduction and the regular costs of operating such a service still need assessment.
[HEADING=1]A fallback strategy, not simply an office-suite swap[/HEADING]
The clearest public explanation of the policy objective is dependency reduction. The federal digital-transformation leadership has characterized the primary goal as creating a genuine fallback option: an alternative that can be used if needed, rather than necessarily replacing Microsoft everywhere.
That makes the project more consequential than a limited software trial, even though its initial scale is modest. A workplace platform that can support ordinary work outside the incumbent environment could give an administration more room to respond to technical disruption, supplier constraints, or policy concerns. It could also make future procurement negotiations less one-sided if it becomes a credible operational alternative.
But a fallback has to work under real conditions to be valuable. It needs more than the ability to open documents. It must support identity and access management, communications, calendars, file handling, collaboration, governance, user support, and continuity during an actual disruption. Running a parallel environment can therefore be a rational resilience investment, but it can also introduce complexity: separate training needs, document-compatibility questions, integration work, duplicated support processes, and new security responsibilities.
The federal program should consequently be judged less by the headline number of users than by whether those users can perform their normal work reliably and whether the alternative can be operated when it is most needed.
[HEADING=1]What the BOSS proof of concept found[/HEADING]
The new phase builds on the BOSS feasibility study, which used openDesk-based software and involved 172 participants from several departments. The testing scope was broad enough to resemble a modern workplace stack rather than a word processor replacement. It included document editing, email, calendars, contacts and tasks, file storage, project and knowledge management, chat, audio and video conferencing, plus identity and access management.
The Federal Chancellery reported positive assessments for key day-to-day functions, including document work, file storage, collaboration, email, and calendars. That is an important result: it suggests the tested environment could support a meaningful set of standard administrative workflows.
At the same time, the findings do not amount to a blanket production-readiness verdict. Large video conferences exposed limitations. This is particularly important because video meetings are one of the areas where organizations often discover the difference between a technically available feature and a service that performs predictably at organizational scale.
The test result therefore supports two conclusions at once. First, a non-Microsoft workplace environment appears viable for a defined range of federal work. Second, substantial implementation, scaling, and operational validation remain necessary before anyone can credibly claim an equivalent substitute for Microsoft 365 across an entire administration.
[HEADING=1]The Microsoft 365 installed-base context[/HEADING]
The program is taking shape after the federal administration completed its Microsoft 365 rollout to approximately 54,000 workplaces in mid-December 2025, according to independent trade reporting. That context underscores why the “replacement” framing is inaccurate.
A 3,000-user parallel deployment is a comparatively bounded program beside that installed base. It may be strategically important without being numerically transformative. Nor should the 3,000-user figure be converted into a device count or a precise percentage of the federal workforce: the official announcement describes users and employees, while the available reporting on Microsoft 365 refers to workplaces. Those are not necessarily like-for-like measures.
For Windows readers, the most practical point is that workplace-software policy and operating-system policy are not the same thing. The announcement concerns a sovereign workplace environment with office functions. It does not establish that 3,000 Windows installations, 3,000 PCs, or the Windows operating system itself will be removed. The available material also does not say that every selected person will permanently abandon Microsoft 365.
That is not a semantic quibble. Device management, security tooling, local application needs, browser compatibility, and identity infrastructure can all shape the experience of using an alternative workplace platform. A parallel service can alter how documents, meetings, mail, and collaboration are handled without constituting an immediate desktop-OS migration.
[HEADING=1]Open source policy is relevant—but not a migration mandate[/HEADING]
Switzerland’s legal framework gives the project a broader policy backdrop. The Federal Act on the Use of Electronic Means to Carry Out Official Tasks, known as EMOTA, entered into force on January 1, 2024. It requires federal authorities to publish the source code of software they develop or commission.
The rule has material exceptions. Code need not be published where third-party rights or security-related reasons prevent or restrict publication.
This law is relevant to public-sector software governance, but it should not be overstated. It does not require the government to replace commercial workplace products. It does not make every government IT component open source. And it does not itself mandate a Microsoft 365 exit.
Its direct scope is software developed or commissioned by federal authorities. The sovereign-workplace program is better understood as a separate operational and strategic initiative that exists within a government taking source-code publication and digital autonomy seriously, not as an automatic legal consequence of EMOTA.
[HEADING=1]The Cyber Command reports need caution[/HEADING]
Separate reporting has linked openDesk to Switzerland’s Cyber Command, but the coverage is not consistent enough to support sweeping conclusions.
One report said that employees with particularly protected identities were expected to receive openDesk workstations by October 2026. A later syndicated account described a broader plan in which all Cyber Command employees would receive openDesk by that date. Because the latter account relies on attributed reporting rather than a located primary Cyber Command announcement, the scope remains unresolved.
The prudent conclusion is that Cyber Command may be pursuing a more focused or accelerated use of openDesk than the 3,000-user federal program. It is not yet safe to state as established fact that every Cyber Command employee is leaving Microsoft Office or Microsoft 365 by October 2026.
This distinction also prevents a specialized security-related deployment from being used as proof that the whole federal administration is about to follow the same timetable.
[HEADING=1]What success would look like by 2027[/HEADING]
The first phase will be more informative than dramatic. Its value lies in testing whether a separate workplace can be made dependable for thousands of people while Microsoft 365 remains in place.
Practical measures of success would include whether staff can complete routine work without unacceptable friction; whether document, mail, calendar, file, and collaboration workflows hold up in normal operations; whether the video-conferencing limitations can be resolved; and whether the organization can support, secure, and govern the service at a predictable cost.
A successful result would strengthen the case for a durable fallback and give the federal government more evidence for the later decision on whether to expand the model. A difficult rollout would not necessarily invalidate the sovereignty goal, but it would demonstrate why office-suite features alone are not enough to replace an established productivity platform.
For now, Switzerland’s move is best described as a carefully scoped resilience experiment with real funding and a clear 2027 milestone. It is a notable challenge to the assumption that a government must depend on one workplace ecosystem. It is not, however, an announced Microsoft 365 replacement for 3,000 computers—or for Switzerland’s federal administration as a whole.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
The U.S. Navy’s reported migration of critical promotion and personnel records from the Millington Data Center to a cloud environment is significant if its stated scope holds. Personnel and promotion information sits close to the core of military administration: it affects careers, readiness reporting, pay-related processes, and confidence in the systems that support service members. But the announcement should be read as a reported milestone and an architectural starting point—not as proof that a long-running modernization problem is finished.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Futuristic military command center links cloud computing, data networks, aircraft, and naval forces."]178295[/ATTACH]
The available record draws an important boundary. The Navy says it completed a move of [I]critical[/I] personnel and promotion records and positions that work as a foundation for Project THETIS, its next-generation human-resources modernization framework. It does not establish that every Millington workload moved, every HR application now runs in the cloud, or that the data center has closed. Nor does it provide the performance, recovery, cost, or independent security evidence needed to substantiate claims of already-realized savings or resilience gains.
[HEADING=1]What the Navy Says Changed[/HEADING]
According to the reported September 3, 2026 announcement, Navy Personnel Command completed a migration of critical Navy promotion and personnel records from the Millington Data Center to a secure cloud environment. The move is described as an initial foundation for Project THETIS, a human-resources modernization initiative led by the Chief of Naval Personnel, Vice Adm. Jeffrey Czerewko.
The reported migration team crossed multiple Navy organizations: MyNavy HR Personnel Systems Management, identified as OPNAV N16; Navy Personnel Command; MyNavy HR IT Solutions, identified as PMW 240; and Navy Information Warfare Systems Atlantic. That mix matters. A personnel-system migration is not simply an infrastructure operation. It requires the organization responsible for policy and records, the program office responsible for technology, and the operational IT organization to agree on what can move, who may access it, how data is protected, and how the service will respond when something fails.
The Navy also describes a cloud architecture built around identity validation, constrained access, encryption, and greater enterprise visibility. Those are sensible design goals for sensitive personnel information. Identity validation is intended to ensure users and systems are truly who they claim to be. Access limitation applies the related principle that even authenticated users should receive only the permissions they need. Encryption helps protect data in transit and at rest. Enterprise visibility can give security and operations teams a better view of systems, access activity, and potential anomalies than a fragmented legacy environment can provide.
Still, these are reported architectural characteristics and intended protections, rather than published evidence of outcomes. There are no supplied results for availability, successful disaster-recovery tests, recovery time, recovery-point targets, security assessments, user disruption, or cost. The Navy’s statement that Sailor data remained secure during the migration is important, but it is not accompanied here by a technical assessment or outside validation.
[HEADING=1]Why “Completed Migration” Has a Narrow Meaning[/HEADING]
The language around a cloud migration can easily imply more than the underlying announcement supports. A completed transfer of critical records may be a major accomplishment. It does not necessarily mean the applications that use those records have been rehosted, rewritten, retired, or proven capable of operating during an outage of the original facility.
That distinction is particularly important for Windows and enterprise IT administrators. Moving data and operating an application are connected but different engineering tasks. A database can be replicated or backed up to cloud storage while the application tier still depends on a legacy server, a particular identity configuration, an older integration, or network paths available only in the original data center. A service is truly more resilient only when the full operating chain has been tested: user authentication, application servers, database access, interfaces with adjacent systems, monitoring, backups, restore procedures, and failover operations.
The reported announcement does not enumerate the migrated applications, databases, record categories, data volume, remaining dependencies, or excluded workloads. It also does not say that the Millington Data Center has been decommissioned, that it no longer runs other Navy systems, or that it has a defined retirement date. Calling this an important first step is therefore more accurate than calling it a total exit from Millington.
This is not semantic caution for its own sake. Data-center retirement, application modernization, and cloud data migration each carry different costs, risks, and definitions of success. An agency can complete one while remaining far from completing the others.
[HEADING=1]The 2025 Context Makes Validation Essential[/HEADING]
Independent reporting in 2025 described a much less mature state for the Navy HR modernization effort. One account said a cloud backup capability existed but was not sufficient to run Millington applications in the cloud. Another reported that a $170 million contract involving Pantheon had been cancelled in early May 2025.
Those reports predate the Navy’s reported September 2026 milestone. They do not directly disprove a later migration. Over more than a year, the Navy could have changed technical approaches, moved different components, found a new contracting route, or delivered capability through other work. It would be wrong to present the 2025 accounts as proof that the 2026 announcement is false.
But the earlier reporting does make an unqualified “problem solved” interpretation difficult to defend. It shows that the gap between having a cloud copy of data and being able to operate applications in the cloud was already recognized as material. It also indicates that program and contracting turbulence were part of the modernization backdrop. A later claim of completion needs to be judged against the precise scope of the work completed, rather than against the broader aspiration of fully modernizing Navy HR.
The unanswered questions are consequential. The available information does not identify whether the new work replaced, incorporated, or otherwise related to the previously cancelled contract. It does not identify the cloud provider, hosting arrangement, authorization level, migration cost, or ongoing operating cost. And it does not show whether the newly reported environment can sustain operations under a genuine site-loss scenario.
[HEADING=1]Project THETIS Should Be Judged as a Service Modernization Effort[/HEADING]
Framing the Millington move as a foundation for Project THETIS offers a more realistic view of what it may represent. Human-resources modernization is not won by relocating records alone. Success depends on whether people, processes, data, and applications can work together reliably at enterprise scale.
For a program such as THETIS, the practical tests will be broader than where data resides. Can authorized users access correct personnel and promotion information when they need it? Are permissions accurate when service members change role, location, or status? Do records remain consistent across the systems that consume them? Can the organization identify an outage quickly and restore critical services within an acceptable period? Can it audit access to highly sensitive personal data? And can it implement change without introducing new errors into career-affecting processes?
The Navy’s stated focus on identity, access limitation, encryption, and visibility addresses several of those concerns at the architectural level. But architecture is not the same as operational proof. For example, stronger identity controls can make a system safer while also creating user-access challenges if role mappings, account recovery, and support processes are not mature. Centralized visibility can improve incident response, but only if logging is complete, alerts are actionable, and personnel have procedures to act on them.
This is also why “technical debt reduction” should remain an expectation rather than a completed result. A cloud environment can reduce the burden of maintaining aging on-premises hardware, but it can also preserve old application assumptions, add cloud-management complexity, and create new integration or cost-control problems. Whether technical debt falls depends on what was modernized beyond the movement of records.
[HEADING=1]What Evidence Would Demonstrate a Durable Improvement[/HEADING]
The Navy does not need to publish sensitive implementation details to show that the effort has produced concrete operational value. Meaningful public indicators could include service availability over time, recovery objectives, completed failover exercises, the percentage of in-scope workloads moved, and a clear description of which legacy infrastructure remains necessary.
Operationally useful evidence would also distinguish between a backup, replicated data, and a fully usable recovery environment. A backup may preserve information. A recovery environment must demonstrate that applications and their dependencies can be restored and operated. A resilient active environment goes further, requiring the ability to maintain or resume services through defined failures. These are different levels of capability, and combining them under the word “cloud” obscures the difference.
Cost claims similarly need context. A migration can involve high near-term engineering, licensing, networking, security, and staffing costs even when it is expected to lower long-term infrastructure risk. Without migration costs, recurring cloud expenditure, legacy-retirement status, and workload performance information, neither savings nor cost increases can be responsibly inferred.
[HEADING=1]Lessons for Windows and Enterprise IT Teams[/HEADING]
The Millington case is a useful reminder for organizations moving Windows-centered business systems from a data center to cloud infrastructure. Do not treat a data move as the finish line. Inventory the application stack and dependencies, including directory services, service accounts, group policies, certificates, file shares, databases, scheduled tasks, network rules, monitoring agents, backup tooling, and third-party integrations.
Identity deserves special attention. Access controls are strongest when they follow real job roles, are reviewed as personnel change, and do not leave behind privileged accounts or brittle emergency-access paths. Encryption and audit logs are valuable, but they do not substitute for restore testing, incident drills, and clear ownership across infrastructure, security, and application teams.
Most importantly, measure outcomes before declaring success. Test that the application—not only its records—can operate after a simulated loss of the original environment. Record how long restoration takes, whether data is current enough for the business process, and where manual workarounds remain. That discipline is as relevant to a mid-sized Windows Server estate as it is to a military personnel system.
[HEADING=1]A Promising Milestone, Not a Final Verdict[/HEADING]
If the Navy’s reported migration has moved critical promotion and personnel records into a protected cloud environment without compromising data, it represents meaningful progress in a sensitive and consequential modernization effort. The multi-organization structure and the connection to Project THETIS suggest the work is intended to support a wider transformation rather than a one-off infrastructure change.
Yet the evidence currently supports a narrower conclusion than the most enthusiastic framing. The reported move covers critical records, not necessarily every application or workload; it is a foundation, not proof of full HR modernization; and its claimed security and resilience benefits have not been matched here with measurable post-migration results. The next meaningful milestone will not be another broad cloud label. It will be evidence that essential personnel services can operate reliably, recover convincingly, and improve for the Sailors and administrators who depend on them.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===

===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
Windows 10 and Windows 11 can run a gaming monitor at 120Hz, 144Hz, 165Hz, 240Hz, or higher only when the entire display chain supports that mode: the monitor, its selected input, the cable, the GPU output, Windows, and the game. Microsoft’s current Display Settings guidance makes the Windows change straightforward, but the common failure is assuming a 144Hz monitor is actually receiving a 144Hz signal because its box says so.
Set the rate in Windows first, then verify it on the monitor itself and inside the game. A frame-rate counter alone cannot prove the display connection is operating at the intended refresh rate.
[HEADING=1][ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="Gaming monitor displays a rainy first-person shooter, with 1440p/165Hz settings and a DisplayPort cable highlighted."]178293[/ATTACH]Choose the correct monitor and refresh rate in Windows[/HEADING]
In Windows 11, open [B]Settings > System > Display > Advanced display[/B]. If more than one display is attached, use the selector at the top of the page to choose the gaming monitor before changing anything. Windows lists the active desktop resolution, the current refresh rate, and whether the selected display supports variable refresh rate.
Under [B]Choose a refresh rate[/B], select the highest rate available for the monitor at its native resolution. For example, choose 1920 × 1080 at 144Hz for a 1080p 144Hz panel, or 2560 × 1440 at 165Hz for a 1440p 165Hz model.
Windows 10 uses a similar route:
[LIST=1]
[*]Open [B]Start > Settings > System > Display[/B].
[*]Select the gaming monitor if you have multiple displays.
[*]Scroll down and choose [B]Advanced display settings[/B].
[*]Select the desired refresh rate from the [B]Refresh rate[/B] list.
[/LIST]
Microsoft notes one easily missed detail: an asterisk beside a refresh-rate option means Windows must change resolution to use it. A monitor might offer 165Hz only at 1920 × 1080, for example, while its native 2560 × 1440 mode tops out at 144Hz through the currently connected input. Do not choose a higher number blindly if it forces a resolution you do not want.
After selecting a new mode, Windows may briefly blank the screen while the monitor renegotiates the signal. Keep the setting when the image returns. If it does not return or looks corrupted, wait for Windows to revert the change automatically.
Windows 10 reached end of support on October 14, 2025. The refresh-rate controls still work, but a gaming PC that remains on Windows 10 should be treated as an unsupported operating-system installation from a security and driver-support perspective.
[HR][/HR]
[HEADING=1]A high-refresh monitor needs a complete signal path[/HEADING]
The list in Windows is not a promise of every mode printed on a monitor’s retail packaging. It is a list of modes the graphics driver believes the current connection can use. If 144Hz, 165Hz, or 240Hz is missing, work backward through the hardware before searching for obscure Windows tweaks.
Start with the monitor’s on-screen display menu. Many gaming monitors have an Information, Input, or Display Status page that shows the current incoming resolution and refresh rate. This is the most useful verification step: Windows may show the selected setting, while the monitor confirms what the panel says it is actually receiving.
Check these items in order:
[LIST]
[*]Use the monitor input that supports its advertised maximum refresh rate at the native resolution. Some displays reserve their highest modes for a particular DisplayPort or HDMI input.
[*]Connect the GPU directly to the monitor where possible. USB-C docks, display adapters, KVM switches, capture devices, and older AV receivers can limit available bandwidth or report a restricted set of display modes.
[*]Use a cable certified or supplied for the needed connection standard, but verify the monitor and GPU manuals rather than relying on a cable label alone. The same “HDMI” label can cover hardware with very different maximum combinations of resolution, refresh rate, color depth, and HDR.
[*]Make sure the cable is connected to the discrete graphics card, not to a motherboard video port, on a desktop PC with a dedicated GPU. Motherboard ports may use integrated graphics or be disabled entirely, depending on the system.
[*]Check the monitor’s own menu for an [I]overclock[/I] or high-refresh setting. A number of displays ship at a lower default limit and expose 165Hz, 180Hz, or higher only after that option is enabled in the monitor firmware menu.
[/LIST]
A 4K monitor is where compromises become especially visible. A connection may carry 4K at 60Hz, 120Hz with reduced color settings, or a lower resolution at a higher rate, depending on the exact monitor, GPU, cable, and input. HDR can also affect which combinations appear because it increases the amount of display data being sent. The correct target is not simply the largest refresh-rate number; it is the monitor’s intended native-resolution mode with the color and HDR settings you actually plan to use.
[HEADING=1]Keep the desktop at the mode you intend to game on[/HEADING]
Set the Windows desktop to the desired native resolution and refresh rate before launching the game. This is particularly important for games that run in borderless windowed mode, because borderless games commonly present through the desktop’s display mode rather than taking exclusive control of the panel.
If the desktop is set to 60Hz, a borderless game can remain tied to that 60Hz presentation path even if the monitor is rated for 144Hz or 165Hz. Changing a game’s graphics preset will not automatically fix the desktop refresh setting.
Avoid testing a high-refresh display while Windows is duplicating the gaming monitor to a TV, projector, capture device, or older secondary display. Duplicated displays can produce confusing mode limits because Windows must find a signal arrangement both devices can accept. Use [B]Extend these displays[/B] for a multi-monitor gaming setup, or temporarily select [B]Show only on 1[/B] or [B]Show only on 2[/B] while diagnosing the gaming monitor.
If Windows still does not offer the expected rate, update the graphics driver from NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel rather than relying only on the version delivered through Windows Update. Driver control panels can also show available modes: NVIDIA Control Panel’s [B]Change resolution[/B] page, for instance, has a refresh-rate selector for the active display. Treat that as a diagnostic cross-check, not a competing configuration to repeatedly toggle back and forth with Windows.
[HR][/HR]
[HEADING=1]Configure the game separately[/HEADING]
A Windows setting establishes what the display can use; the game still needs to render and present correctly. Open the game’s [B]Display[/B], [B]Video[/B], or [B]Graphics[/B] settings and check four items: display mode, monitor selection, resolution, and refresh rate.
Select the correct physical monitor first. Games can open on the wrong screen when a TV, laptop panel, or second monitor is connected. Then choose the same native resolution and target refresh rate selected in Windows, if the game provides an explicit refresh-rate menu.
For first testing, use fullscreen or exclusive fullscreen if the game offers it. This removes some uncertainty around borderless-window behavior and makes the selected in-game display mode easier to identify. Once the high-refresh signal is confirmed, switch back to borderless if you prefer faster Alt+Tab behavior or multi-monitor convenience.
V-Sync, frame caps, and variable refresh rate solve different problems:
[LIST]
[*]V-Sync can cap the game’s presentation rate to the display refresh rate and reduce tearing, but it does not turn a 60Hz connection into a 144Hz one.
[*]A frame-rate cap below the monitor’s refresh rate can be intentional, especially for power, heat, noise, or frame-time consistency. It also means the game will not supply a new frame on every 144Hz or 165Hz refresh interval.
[*]Variable refresh rate, including AMD FreeSync and NVIDIA G-SYNC Compatible operation, lets a supported display vary its refresh timing to track the game’s delivered frames within the monitor’s supported range. It is valuable when the frame rate moves around, but it does not replace selecting the right maximum refresh rate in Windows.
[/LIST]
Microsoft says Windows 11’s Dynamic Refresh Rate can vary the rate automatically on supported hardware, primarily to balance smoothness and battery life. It is not available in Windows 10. On a desktop gaming monitor, the practical check remains the selected mode in Advanced display and the monitor’s own input-status screen.
[HEADING=1]Verify smooth gameplay instead of trusting one number[/HEADING]
Use three separate checks after applying the setting.
First, return to [B]Advanced display[/B] and confirm Windows reports the intended refresh rate for the correct monitor. Second, open the monitor’s on-screen information page and confirm that it reports the same incoming signal—for example, 2560 × 1440 at 165Hz. Third, check the game’s own display settings and performance overlay.
The game’s frames-per-second counter answers a different question from the monitor’s status page. If a game runs at 72 fps on a 144Hz monitor, Windows and the monitor can still be configured correctly; the GPU is simply delivering half as many frames as the panel can refresh. Lower graphics settings, a performance-focused upscaling mode, or a sensible frame cap may improve the experience, depending on the game and hardware.
Conversely, a game reporting 200 fps does not prove a 200Hz display signal. A 60Hz monitor can receive more frames from the GPU than it can physically show. The monitor status page and Windows Advanced display page are the checks that establish whether the connection is actually running at 120Hz, 144Hz, 165Hz, or beyond.
The final practical outcome should be easy to state: Windows shows the target rate, the monitor’s own menu confirms the matching input signal, and the game is running on that monitor at an appropriate resolution and display mode. If any one of those three disagrees, the high-refresh setup is not finished.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
Hi This Wreckage. The screenshot confirms that [B][ICODE]ToolkitCo.exe[/ICODE] is failing to start[/B]. Error [ICODE]0xc0000142[/ICODE] means a DLL failed to initialize; it does not identify the underlying cause. [B]I can’t reliably identify the program from its filename alone[/B], so let’s check what it belongs to before disabling anything.
[HEADING=2]Identify the startup entry[/HEADING]
[LIST=1]
[*]Press [B]Ctrl + Shift + Esc[/B] to open Task Manager.
[*]Click [B]More details[/B], if shown, then the [B]Startup[/B] tab. This lists applications configured to launch when you sign in.
[*]Look for [B]ToolkitCo[/B] or an entry containing [B]Toolkit[/B]. If you find one, right-click it and select [B]Open file location[/B].
[*]Right-click the highlighted file and select [B]Properties[/B]. Check [B]Details[/B] for its product name and company, and [B]Digital Signatures[/B], if present, for the signer.
[*]Reply with the [B]file’s full folder path, product name and publisher[/B], or screenshots of those details. If there is no matching startup entry, post a screenshot of the Startup tab instead.
[/LIST]
[HEADING=2]Stopping the popup[/HEADING]
Once we confirm that the entry belongs to an optional application you don’t need at sign-in, the simplest workaround is to [B]disable that specific startup entry[/B], then restart. Task Manager supports [B]Disable[/B] and [B]Enable[/B], so the change is reversible. This stops its automatic launch rather than repairing the application.
[B]Leave it enabled until identified[/B], particularly if it might handle backups or another function you rely on. No registry changes or file deletion are needed at this stage.
===WFTUI-POST-BOUNDARY===
Windows 11’s next wave is less a clean handoff from 25H2 to 26H2 than a continuing stream of features delivered through monthly updates, controlled rollouts, and Insider testing. That distinction matters. A feature shown in a 26H2 discussion may already be technically compatible with 24H2 or 25H2, may be available only to a fraction of eligible PCs, or may still be an experiment with no commitment to ship broadly.
[ATTACH type="thumbnail" align="right" alt="A person stands between futuristic blue and purple digital worlds filled with technology icons."]178290[/ATTACH]
For Windows users deciding whether to install an optional preview update, join an Insider channel, or simply wait, the useful question is not “Which version has the feature?” It is: [B]which release channel has it, what are its limits, and is it ready for everyday use?[/B]
[HEADING=1]26H2 is an enablement update, not a hard feature boundary[/HEADING]
Windows 11 version 26H2 entered the Release Preview Channel on August 27, 2026, with general availability planned later in the year. But Microsoft says that Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 share a servicing branch. Version 26H2 is delivered through an enablement package rather than a wholly separate platform release.
That architecture has an important consequence: features are not necessarily held back until a PC changes its annual Windows version label. Microsoft can deliver them in monthly servicing updates across the shared branch, then turn them on gradually. A PC on 24H2 or 25H2 may therefore receive parts of the same experience being discussed in connection with 26H2.
For users, this is potentially less disruptive than a major operating-system upgrade. An enablement package generally means a smaller transition for eligible PCs because much of the underlying code has already arrived through servicing. For IT teams, it also means version numbers alone are a poor inventory shorthand for feature availability. Deployment planning needs to account for update build, channel, policy configuration, and whether a gradual rollout has reached a given device.
It also means Windows feature coverage will look uneven for a while. Two otherwise similar PCs can be on the same version and have different interfaces or settings because one has received a controlled feature rollout and the other has not.
[HEADING=1]The taskbar becomes movable again, with meaningful caveats[/HEADING]
The most immediately visible change in the August 27 optional preview update, KB5120998, is expanded taskbar positioning. Windows 11 can place the taskbar at the bottom, top, left, or right edge of the display. The update also introduces a smaller-taskbar option.
This answers a long-running practical complaint from people who prefer a top-mounted taskbar for ultrawide displays, a vertical taskbar for document work, or a more compact bar to recover screen space on smaller laptops. It is not merely cosmetic: taskbar location affects pointer travel, the usable height of applications, and how well a desktop layout fits a particular workflow.
However, the design is not equally capable in every position. In this rollout, the Search box and smaller-taskbar mode are supported only when the taskbar is positioned at the top or bottom. Someone moving the taskbar to the left or right should not expect the complete set of new taskbar controls.
There is a second and more fundamental limitation: KB5120998 is an [B]optional preview update[/B], and Microsoft is introducing its new experiences through a gradual rollout. Installing the update does not guarantee that every advertised setting immediately appears. Controlled rollout is a deliberate phased process, not necessarily a failed installation or a local configuration mistake.
That makes the update best suited to users comfortable testing forthcoming Windows changes. It is not a reason for every home user or managed organization to rush an optional preview package onto production machines.
[HEADING=1]Search is being simplified, but with more controls over suggestions[/HEADING]
KB5120998 also changes Windows Search in ways that affect everyday navigation. Microsoft describes a simplified Search home, clearer provenance for results, and a setting that governs web and Microsoft Store suggestions alongside local results. It also adds automatic indexing for commonly used folders.
The provenance change is a useful transparency improvement. Search results can originate from local files, installed applications, the web, or store-related recommendations, and clearer labeling can help users understand why a particular result appeared. That is especially valuable when someone expects a local document and instead receives an online suggestion.
The setting for web and Store suggestions gives users a more direct choice about how much external content participates in routine search. The dossier does not establish that Search becomes completely offline-only, nor should users assume every result category can be disabled independently. Still, a control over those suggestions is a meaningful step for people who want local work to remain the center of the experience.
Automatic indexing of commonly used folders may make frequently accessed files easier to find, but indexing also has practical trade-offs. It can change what Windows treats as readily searchable and may matter to users who keep large working folders outside the usual locations. The value will depend on whether Windows identifies the folders that actually matter to a given workflow.
As with the taskbar changes, these Search features are gradual-rollout experiences in an optional preview update, not a universal entitlement immediately after patching.
[HEADING=1]Preview-update risk is real, not theoretical[/HEADING]
The August preview update should not be framed as an unqualified usability upgrade. Microsoft added known issues between September 2 and September 4 affecting mouse personalization in non-English environments, Teams and Outlook launches on ARM-based systems, and desktop-background settings.
That does not mean every affected PC will encounter a problem, but it changes the sensible risk calculation. Users on ARM hardware who rely on Teams or Outlook should be particularly cautious. Those using non-English Windows configurations or carefully managed desktop backgrounds should also avoid assuming this preview update is harmless.
For most people, the conservative route is to let a feature graduate through regular servicing unless a specific new control solves an immediate problem. Organizations should test the preview update against their language packs, device architectures, business applications, background-management tools, and support workflows before wider deployment.
